articles.title: Video games in cognitive event-related EEG research: A scoping review
articles.authors: Belinda Fleischmann; Sean Mulready; Dirk Ostwald
articles.abstract: Event-related EEG research has traditionally relied on controlled laboratory tasks with limited ecological validity. Video games offer a middle ground between laboratory and real-world settings, combining intuitive interaction with experimental control. This scoping review, reported according to PRISMA-ScR, characterizes video game paradigms used in event-related EEG research and relates their findings to canonical laboratory effects. Database and supplementary searches identified 29 studies using 26 paradigms. Most paradigms used custom-built games and required visuomotor navigation or targeting within continuous gameplay, and most analyses were time-locked to feedback events such as hits or collisions. Findings showed selective convergence with laboratory effects, particularly for P3-like positivities sensitive to event probability, outcome magnitude, and player relevance, and for movement-related activity. Evidence for error- and feedback-related components was more limited, while early sensory responses were rarely examined. We discuss emerging patterns in the use of video games as event-related EEG paradigms, the correspondence between game-elicited and laboratory EEG effects, and the methodological challenges of studying event-related activity during gameplay. In sum, this synthesis aims to guide the selection and design of game paradigms, inform expectations about neural responses during gameplay, and support their interpretation in light of established laboratory findings in future research in this emerging field.

articles.title: Testing the psychometric properties of depression and social-emotional functioning measures with autistic adolescents and their parents
articles.authors: My H Vu; Elika Parab; Vana Matevosian; Pia Hernandez; Jessica Schwartzman
articles.abstract: Autistic youth are a prevalent population in the U.S. facing greater risks for depression and adverse mental health outcomes than the general population of youth. The psychometric properties of most measures remain untested with autistic youth even though autism is characterized by significant heterogeneity including unique cognitive, affective, behavioral and sensory needs. The present study tested the internal consistency, confirmatory factor analysis, convergent and discriminant validity, and cross-informant agreement between 101 autistic adolescents (14-17 years old) and their parents for several depression and social-emotional functioning measures (e.g., social motivation, anhedonia/apathy). Most measures showed acceptable-to-good internal consistency across informants, while confirmatory factor analyses yielded mixed evidence of structural validity. Convergent validity was moderate and adolescent and parent reports agreed poorly to moderately, which emphasizes the value of collecting both perspectives. Findings inform clinical practice by supporting the continued use of several measures in autistic adolescents, while suggesting caution in interpreting others.

articles.title: Barriers to professional mental health help-seeking and considerations for school-based interventions among Secondary School adolescents: an exploratory qualitative study
articles.authors: Christianah Dada
articles.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Professional mental health service use remains low among adolescents, and school-based interventions are frequently designed without consulting the young people and clinicians they are intended to serve. This exploratory qualitative study investigated the specific barriers to professional mental health help-seeking among Nigerian adolescents to inform the development of a culturally relevant school-based intervention. Following the ethical principles of the Belmont Report, a focus group discussion was conducted with ten secondary school students (aged 13–16), alongside individual in-depth interviews with two students and key informant interviews with two practicing clinical psychologists in Ibadan, Nigeria. Audio-recorded transcripts were verified and examined utilizing thematic analysis. Eight core categories emerged from the data, highlighting a limited formal understanding of mental health among youth and a prominent gap between baseline knowledge and help-seeking behaviors. While distress including depression, anxiety, addiction, and trauma was widely recognized through behavioral or academic declines, pervasive stigma and the fear of diagnostic labeling acted as dominant barriers to care, with nine out of ten adolescents refusing professional care pathways. Friends served as primary confidants, while parental spiritual beliefs heavily gatekept formal psychological interventions. Social media heavily informed adolescent self-image but introduced acute body-image concerns. Notably, one student preferred using an artificial intelligence chatbot over human contact to ensure absolute confidentiality. Participants requested foundational mental health literacy and coping skills delivered via brief, visual, interactive sessions, while clinicians anticipated systemic institutional implementation challenges regarding school leadership, funding deficits, and staffing constraints. Interventions must target social stigma and privacy constraints directly alongside conceptual awareness.

articles.title: Commitment-Driven Information Seeking in Misinformation Consumption
articles.authors: Alessandro Miani; Théo Schöpfer; Stephan Lewandowsky; Thomas Hills; Adrian Bangerter
articles.abstract: The role of social media in misinformation consumption remains contested. This disagreement might arise from the failure to distinguish incidental exposure to misinformation from deliberate consumption. We address this gap by analyzing incoming traffic data, collected in November 2020, to more than 2,000 websites that vary in misinformation and type of bias (liberal, conservative, and conspiracy). We compare the traffic modalities through which users reach those sites: direct traffic, such as typing a URL or using a bookmark (mostly associated with self-directed information seeking); social traffic, from links clicked on social media; and search traffic, from search engines (mostly associated with incidental exposure). We found that reliable, low-misinformation websites are reached mainly via search traffic, whereas unreliable ones are mostly reached via direct traffic; this pattern is stronger for conspiracy websites. Breaking down social traffic by platform reveals that Facebook was the main driver of traffic towards unreliable websites, mostly towards politically biased and entry-level conspiracy websites. These findings suggest that structural interventions such as algorithmic adjustments and content moderation may reduce incidental exposure among users with low belief commitment, but are unlikely to deter highly committed information seekers, who require targeted, ideologically informed strategies.

articles.title: Is a joke funnier if it is told by a man? A novel paradigm using AI-generated voices
articles.authors: Amy Zhao
articles.abstract: The stereotype that “men are funnier than women” is culturally pervasive. In a large preregistered online study (n=966), participants rated 12 jokes delivered by a male or female AI-generated voice. To control for differences in delivery, cadence, and intonation, we used a speech-to-speech transformation to transform jokes spoken by a female into a male version and vice versa. Using a Bayesian analysis, we found strong evidence that the apparent gender of the speaker does not affect the perceived funniness of the joke (BF=0.023). We found no interaction between the original and apparent voice gender on masculinity ratings, indicating that vocal gender cues were effectively eliminated when voices were transformed to the opposite gender, reinforcing the merit of this gender manipulation method. Further, men had significantly higher agreement that being funny is a masculine trait than women (MD=0.73, padj<.001), and participants with more male than female friends had significantly higher agreement with this belief than those with equal numbers of male and female friends (MD=0.68, padj<.001) or more female than male friends (MD=0.91, padj<.001). In all, apparent vocal gender does not appear to influence humour evaluations directly, but exploratory findings suggest the apparent vocal gender and delivery may shape broader impressions of speakers (such as perceived confidence and charisma). And individual differences such as gender and proportion of male friends may shape gendered attitudes and expectations toward humour.

articles.title: Toward Distinguishing Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load and Acute Stress in Virtual Reality: Two Randomized and Controlled Studies
articles.authors: Alexis D. Souchet; Mamadou Lamarana Diallo; Mohammad Soleymani; Domitile Lourdeaux
articles.abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is increasingly used to study Cognitive load and Acute Stress. But VR comes with side effects such as Cybersickness and Visual fatigue. It remains unclear if we can dissociate psychophysiological responses due to confounding effects. Hence, we conducted two experiments to study and distinguish them. Participants fulfilled a Baseline, Stroop task under four different experimental conditions, Relaxation and Endline. We recorded Stroop performances, Eye tracking (ET), Electrocardiography (ECG), Electrodermal activity (EDA), self-reported Cognitive load, Stress, Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, and Disorientation. Pupil diameter, Blink frequency, Fixations, HR, HRV, and Skin Conductance Response derived between the different conditions. Most of the extracted features from ET, ECG, and EDA showed no differences between states. Despite relaxation steps, Saccade ratio, Blink frequency, Blink duration and Pupil size for ET, Heart rate for ECG, Rise time of the mean skin conductance level, the Arc length of the skin conductance level for EDA were still not back equivalent to baseline. Cognitive load differs from Acute stress based on the Heart rate feature from the ECG sensor. Cognitive load provoked more response with EDA features than Visual fatigue / Cybersickness with the ALSC feature. However, most of those differences have small effect sizes. We underline a 60 minutes immersion “limit.” ET was more sensitive to Visual fatigue / Cybersickness compared to Cognitive load and Acute Stress and ECG to Cognitive load compared to Acute Stress. We documented physiological features varying depending on the state and which one allowed their differentiation. However, side effects can confound other state measures; especially the longer participants are immersed. More experimental inputs are necessary to tackle this research question.

articles.title: Perceiving Interceptive Affordances: How Target Distance, Target Speed and Additional Load Shape Interception Decisions in Football
articles.authors: John Oyewole; Wiktoria Moskal; Hatty Jones; Harry Ramsey; Helen Nuttall; Christopher Gaffney; Trevor J. Crawford; Sally Linkenauger
articles.abstract: To perform well, athletes must perceive both individual and social affordances within sporting environments. Interceptive action is often crucial to sporting success, yet research investigating interceptive affordance perception in open-play competitive sporting environments is extremely limited. This novel research investigates how factors such as target distance, target speed, and additional load jointly influence affordance perception for interceptive actions against opponents. Across three pre-registered studies, university level footballers (n = 26) made action-based judgments on whether they could successfully intercept a target moving perpendicularly towards the space between themselves and an opponent. The position of the target systematically varied in its proximity to the participant versus the opponent. Participants consistently displayed proactive interceptive behaviour, persisting with manipulations to target speed, and additional load applied to players and opponents. However, exploratory mixed-effects modelling revealed that participants were sensitive to increases in relative target distance, and additional load, but less sensitive to increases in target speed. These findings have wide ranging implications across many sporting and non-sporting contexts, providing new insights to understanding affordance perception in competitive sporting situations and other fast-paced environments. Additionally, this work has practical applications, highlighting opportunities to explore coaching interventions to enhance interceptive decision-making during matches.

articles.title: Building Research Infrastructure for Meaningful Youth Participation: A Practice-Informed Framework for Participatory Research
articles.authors: Vera Ellen Heininga; Marloes Dekkers
articles.abstract:
Background: While current frameworks present essential principles for effective youth involvement, they provide limited practical advice on how participation can be organized and maintained throughout research projects. Meaningful involvement requires not just chances for youth to engage, but also the structural, relational, and procedural conditions that allow them to have real impact.
Objective: This paper intends to present a practice-based framework for developing research infrastructure that enables meaningful youth involvement and to demonstrate its use across the research process.
Methods: Building upon fifteen years of hands-on experience in youth engagement at Jimmy’s, we adapt a practice-based ecosystem-based model into a framework for participatory research, guided by equity principles and Lundy’s child participation model. The Youth Resilience Groningen study acts as a practical example to demonstrate how this framework can guide the organization of youth engagement, encompassing the formation of partnerships, defined roles, resources, facilitation, co-design, and decision-making processes.
Results: The framework places equity as its main guiding principle and outlines four interrelated pillars: the research organization, researchers and research personnel, emerging research collaborators, and the broader network of community and research allies. These pillars are formed through three parallel processes: Doing, Learning, and Organising. In the Youth Resilience Groningen study, six teens were hired as junior researchers, aided by Jimmy’s, and participated in determining research priorities, creating study materials, developing questionnaires, planning recruitment strategies, and developing educational guest lectures for secondary school classes, delivered as a token of appreciation for their participation in the study. The study demonstrates how organizational structures and continuous support can enable youth participation while addressing ethical, methodological, and institutional limitations.
Conclusion: Effective youth engagement goes beyond just including young individuals in research efforts. It relies on an ecosystem that allows their insights and viewpoints to guide research choices. The practice-based framework provides flexible direction for structuring, overseeing, and enhancing meaningful youth participation in research projects.

articles.title: Nine-Year Changes in Work Satisfaction in Midlife – the Role of Age and Flexible Goal Adjustment
articles.authors: Georg Henning; Nadiya Kelle; Frank J Infurna
articles.abstract: As the work force is ageing and many countries raise or abolish retirement ages, it becomes more and more important to understand how work satisfaction develops over the lifespan, particularly in midlife and older age. Although many studies report positive associations of age and work satisfaction, there are only few longitudinal studies with large samples investigating within-person change over longer time spans. To overcome these limitations, we used data from the German Ageing Survey to investigate changes in work satisfaction among n = 2,588 individuals aged 40 – 59 at four measurement occasions between 2008 and 2017. As our study was informed by life span approaches to self-regulation at work, we were also interested in the role of age and flexible goal adjustment, which is the ability to adjust one’s goals according to restrictions in the environment. Results showed that work satisfaction was characterized by stability in midlife, but workers in their 60’s experienced increases in work satisfaction. Nevertheless, these effects may partly show selection effects due to dissatisfied older workers retiring over time and / or dropping out of the survey. Flexible goal adjustment was related to higher work satisfaction, but not to changes in work satisfaction. Our results demonstrate that work satisfaction can increase in older age and that flexible goal adjustment may play a role in shaping the course of work satisfaction in midlife and older age. More research is needed to understand which coping mechanisms help aging workers to stay satisfied at work.

articles.title: How Many Sites, Participants, and Trials? A Tutorial on Multilevel Power Analysis for Multisite Studies with Repeated Measures
articles.authors: Alicia Franco-Martínez; Miguel A. Vadillo; Ricardo Rey-Sáez
articles.abstract: Multisite collaborations are increasingly common in psychological science. Planning a multisite study with repeated measures involves more than deciding how many participants to recruit. Researchers must also determine how many sites to include and how many observations to collect from each participant. These decisions become particularly challenging when the experimental effect may vary across both participants and sites. Unfortunately, most widely used power analysis tools do not accommodate the complexity of these structures. In this tutorial, we provide a practical introduction to multilevel power analysis for three-level multisite studies. We first discuss how to identify and model the effect of interest, accounting for different sources of heterogeneity and the population to which researchers intend to generalize their findings. We then demonstrate how to estimate statistical power through simulation using {simr} and how to optimize the number of trials, participants, and sites using {mlpwr}, considering their relative costs. Finally, we illustrate how to explore alternative assumptions about effect size and between-site heterogeneity, verify the power of the selected architecture, assess estimation precision, and calculate the minimum detectable effect size. The accompanying R code provides an adaptable workflow to help researchers plan multisite studies that balance their inferential goals with their available resources.

articles.title: How Does Chatbot Anthropomorphism Shape Psychological Reactance? An Experiment on Trust and Perceived Persuasive Intent in Vaping Cessation Conversations
articles.authors: Xingman Wu
articles.abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly used to deliver health information and persuasive interventions, yet the consequences of making these systems appear humanlike remain unclear. Drawing on the Computers Are Social Actors and Media Are Social Actors paradigms, mind perception theory, and psychological reactance theory, this research examined whether anthropomorphism in AI chatbots shapes reactance through two competing pathways: trust in the chatbot and perceived persuasive intent. An online between-subjects experiment was conducted among U.S. adults who currently used e-cigarettes. Participants in the main study (N = 586) were randomly assigned to interact with either an anthropomorphic or a non-anthropomorphic AI chatbot, or to view a static vaping cessation message. The results showed that interacting with an anthropomorphized chatbot reduced reactance compared to reading a static message, although this advantage did not extend to attitudes toward vaping or intentions to quit. Additionally, while anthropomorphism can generally reduce psychological reactance, its two dimensions, mindful and mindless anthropomorphism, operated in different paths. Mindful anthropomorphism was associated with greater trust and, indirectly, lower reactance. Mindless anthropomorphism was directly associated with lower reactance. These findings support the potential use of anthropomorphic AI chatbots as a communication approach for vaping cessation. Furthermore, by distinguishing mindful from mindless anthropomorphism and clarifying their distinct mechanisms, this research offers a more nuanced explanation of how humanlike AI cues shape psychological reactance and provides practical guidance for designing AI-mediated health interventions.

articles.title: Psychometric Properties and Diagnostic Accuracy of Spanish BESA Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition in Mexican Children
articles.authors: Reinaldo Cabrera Pérez; Alejandra Auza
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Accurate identification of developmental language disorder (DLD) requires assessment measures validated for their intended populations. This study examined the psychometric properties and diagnostic accuracy of preliminary Spanish grammatical measures from the Bilingual English–Spanish Assessment (BESA) in monolingual Mexican children. Method: Participants included 395 monolingual Spanish-speaking children aged 3;0–5;5 years (295 typically developing, 100 with DLD). Twenty-two grammatical cloze items and 53 sentence repetition targets were examined using regression, classical item analyses, item response theory, receiver operating characteristic analyses, and repeated cross-validation.
Results: Children with DLD performed significantly below typically developing children on both tasks, while scores increased with age. Clitic pronouns and subjunctive constructions demonstrated strong item-level discrimination, and two-parameter item response models fit better than one-parameter models. The 21-item Morphosyntax score yielded an area under the curve of .872, compared with .847 for the 29-target Sentence Repetition score. Combining both tasks yielded .885, although the improvement in discrimination was not statistically significant. Discussion: Findings provide promising evidence of the diagnostic utility of preliminary BESA Spanish grammatical measures in monolingual Mexican children and highlight the importance of item-level evaluation and population-specific validity evidence. Further research is needed to evaluate the complete published assessment, establish clinical cutoffs, and compare item performance across monolingual and bilingual populations.

articles.title: From motivation to experience: Blurred boundaries in the measurement of adolescent social media engagement
articles.authors: Margarita Panayiotou; Emily Banwell; Louise Black; Jo Hickman Dunne; Jade Davies; Suzanne Hamilton; Brittany I Davidson; Lukas J. Gunschera; Amanda Iselin Olesen Andersen; Turi Reiten Finserås
articles.abstract: Despite extensive research on the role of social media use in adolescent mental health, fundamental questions remain about what current self-report measures capture. We systematically reviewed 96 adolescent self-report measures of social media use, comprising 1,526 unique items. Through content analysis, we examined what measures assess and the behavioural and psychological processes through which they are operationalised. We found substantial conceptual overlap between measures, particularly those assessing problematic use and addiction, alongside discrepancies between item content and young people’s reported experiences. Importantly, current measures were found to frequently combine motivation, behaviour, experience, and mindset, despite these psychological behaviours and processes being theoretically distinguished. This raises questions about whether existing measures meaningfully test the hypothesises mechanisms and theoretical frameworks underpinning social media and mental health research. Our findings highlight the need to move beyond content-focused approaches to measurement, towards greater attention to how social media is operationalised and recognition of its potentially dynamic and interdependent nature.

articles.title: Preliminary Psychometric Analysis of an Online Diagnostic Assessment of Statistical Reasoning for Psychology Students: A Cognitive Psychology Perspective
articles.authors: Dina Nazriani; Suri Mutia Siregar; Dian Ulfasari Pasaribu; Fasti Rola
articles.abstract: Digital tools make diagnostic tests easy to build, but convenience does not guarantee that scores reflect the intended thinking processes. This study examined item quality and reliability of Draft 1 of the Statistical Reasoning Diagnostic Assessment for Psychology Students (SRDA-PSY), an online two-tier diagnostic test covering six domains of statistical reasoning, interpreting the results through cognitive psychology principles. Forty-one psychology students took the test via Google Forms. Classical test theory analyses (difficulty, discrimination, distractor effectiveness, two-tier response patterns, and KR-20) were triangulated with a single expert review. The mean score was 83%, and 26 of 41 items were very easy. All 15 items of moderate or easy difficulty discriminated well, but only 21% of distractors were functional. The key was the longest option in 57 of 63 option sets, and the six items without this cue were much harder (mean p = .53 vs. .89), suggesting that many items could be answered with an option-form heuristic rather than analytic reasoning. On two-tier items, students often endorsed a correct general principle but failed to apply it to the case, consistent with the view that intuitive and scientific conceptions can coexist. KR-20 was .90 but dropped to .78 when the two lowest-scoring respondents were removed, and expert review and empirical data detected different weaknesses. The content of SRDA-PSY is promising, but option form must be revised so that scores reflect statistical reasoning. Digital assessment development, including AI-assisted item writing, should combine expert review, empirical tryouts, and automated audits of option-form cues.

articles.title: Public Skepticism about AI Consciousness
articles.authors: Ali Ladak; Lucius Caviola
articles.abstract: Most people think that current AI systems, such as ChatGPT, lack consciousness—the capacity for subjective experience. But what about future AI systems so advanced that their behavior, appearance, and functionality are indistinguishable from humans? Across one main and four supplementary preregistered experiments (total N = 3,455), participants imagined interacting with such systems in hypothetical future scenarios. On average, people remain deeply skeptical: they attribute very low levels of consciousness to even the most advanced AI, comparable to an ant and far below a chimpanzee or a human. Still, several factors increased consciousness attributions. Ratings rose when experts endorsed the system’s consciousness, when participants formed an emotional connection during interaction, when the system was described as an exact digital copy of a human brain, and when it had a physical body. The largest effect occurred when the AI was depicted as gradually transitioning from a human while retaining memories and other psychological traits. Although average attributions were low, variability was high for the more advanced systems: many participants gave very low ratings, while others gave very high ones. This polarization suggests that as AI systems become more capable and human-like, public views about their potential consciousness could diverge sharply.

articles.title: The Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ):  Measuring Individual Differences in Song Listening
articles.authors: Dominique T Vuvan; Julia Cannistraro; Rachel Goodkind; Megha Sharda
articles.abstract: Recent years have seen a significant increase in the use of songs, which contain an integrated music/language signal, as experimental stimuli. This has created a need for standardized tools to measure individual differences in song perception. The current article reports the development of the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), which measures the degree to which a song listener’s cognitive resources are oriented towards the lyrics versus the other musical features (i.e., pitch, rhythm, timbre). In Study 1, we used exploratory factor analysis to reduce 121 candidate items down to 12 items for the LFQ. In Study 2, we used confirmatory factor analysis and internal consistency measures to ascertain the unidimensional structure of the LFQ. In Studies 3 and 4, we demonstrated that the LFQ is correlated to comprehension of lyrics but not to the ability to exactly recall lyrics. In Study 5, we aggregated data from the first four studies to create initial norms for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire and to explore discriminant validity between Lyric Focus and musical and literary activities with more statistical power than in each study alone. The LFQ is presented as a practical, valid, and reliable tool for researchers interested in the relation between music and language.

articles.title: Mechanical and Psychological Domains of Thought are Analogically Asymmetrical
articles.authors: Martin Meyer; Frank Keil
articles.abstract: Psychology and physics are two core domains of human cognition. Little is known about their epistemic relation. Does our understanding of common physical-mechanical systems better inform our understanding of psychology, or vice versa? To answer this question, we compared analogies that explain one domain in terms of the other. In Study 1, we found the best analogies with a mechanical base explaining a psychological target were preferred to the best analogies in the opposite direction. In Study 2, we generated analogies from random pairings of mechanical and psychological systems and again found a preference for analogies with a mechanical base. In Study 3, participants overwhelmingly generated analogies with a mechanical (instead of psychological) base. And Study 4 showed that analogies with a mechanical base were also preferred to those with bases from other domains. These results suggest that the physical-mechanical domain may serve as a privileged launchpad for explanation.

articles.title: Everything that quacks ain't a duck. What can we learn from phonetic distributions?
articles.authors: Huanbin Teng; Karthik Durvasula
articles.abstract: Phonetic studies sometimes infer how many categories a linguistic system contains using surface distributional diagnostics. This inference is examined by distinguishing four levels: distribution shape, labeled-group separation, statistical components, and linguistic categories. In an equal-proportion, equal-variance Gaussian mixture, two speech categories produce a unimodal pooled distribution when the distance between their means is less than two standard deviations. In many realistic contexts, unimodality of a pooled distribution alone does not establish the presence of a single linguistic category. Conversely, bimodality of a pooled distribution alone does not establish two linguistic categories. The standard mixture-variance decomposition also shows that a two-category mixture need not have greater variance than its more variable component. Simulations show mode-based diagnostics can correctly describe surface modality yet poorly recover the categories that generated the data. Empirical cases further illustrate that distribution shape, labeled-group separation, and component structure capture distinct properties of the data and need not converge on the same category analysis. These diagnostics should thus be interpreted at their own levels. Agreement among them can strengthen a description of surface structure, but they cannot determine categoryhood on their own. Category-level claims require converging linguistic evidence suited to the category under study.

articles.title: Open research materials need explicit reuse licenses
articles.authors: Björn S. Siepe; Daniel W. Heck; Daniel S Quintana
articles.abstract: Researchers increasingly share materials online, but often without a license, which means others cannot tell how they may reuse them. Because materials often outlive their authors' involvement, reuse questions can go unanswered. Licensing takes minutes, at the point of sharing or years later, and authors should act while they can still edit their materials.

articles.title: New Voices for Environmental Causes: The Psychological Basis of Different Reactions to Posts by Human and Virtual Greenfluencers
articles.authors: Nils Burgheim; Cornelia Sindermann
articles.abstract:
The present paper systematically investigates audience reactions to posts by human greenfluencers versus virtual greenfluencers controlled by humans or AI. Drawing on persuasion theory and research, we hypothesized that posts by human versus human-controlled versus AI-controlled virtual influencers and gender-congruent influencers are rated as more credible and that these variables may also be linked to engagement intentions. Furthermore, we expected that trust in humans and trust in AI are positively related to the perceived credibility of posts of the respective influencer type. We explored relations with engagement intentions exploratorily.
In a 3×2-mixed online experiment, N = 343 participants were presented either with posts by (i) human greenfluencers, (ii) human-controlled virtual greenfluencers, or (iii) AI-controlled virtual greenfluencers. Each participant further saw posts by a greenfluencer depicting (i) a man and (ii) a woman. Participants self-reported perceived credibility and engagement intentions with each post. 
Results show that while gender congruency had no significant effects, participants rated human greenfluencer posts as most credible compared to posts by both virtual greenfluencer types. Engagement intentions did not differ between greenfluencer types. Trust in AI emerged as a relevant but nuanced predictor of the different outcomes for different greenfluencer types.
As virtual greenfluencers become more prevalent, differences in reactions to them versus human greenfluencers may attenuate. Given their scalability, it thus remains important to examine when and for whom virtual greenfluencers and their posts may elicit comparable or even stronger reactions than human greenfluencers.

articles.title: Which memory does brain stimulation improve? The priming problem
articles.authors: Halil Aziz Velioglu; murat can çelik; Dogukan Aslan; Mehmet Akif Sakiroglu; Yusuf Çiçek; Ali Tarik Altunc
articles.abstract: Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of cortical sites connected with the hippocampus improves scores on episodic memory tests and is being tested for memory decline, including in Alzheimer's disease. These gains are read as gains in intentional retrieval. Objective: To examine whether standard memory outcomes can support this reading and how the contribution of repetition priming can be measured. Methods: Narrative review of hippocampal-network stimulation studies, cognitive and electrophysiological research on priming and processing fluency, stimulation studies of priming and parietal cortex, and clinical trials of TMS for memory decline. Results: Old/new recognition and cued recall present studied items or cues again at test. Repetition priming makes these items easier to process, and this fluency can raise a memory score with intentional retrieval unchanged. The fluency behind word-recognition decisions is largely conceptual, so it persists after a change of surface form. TMS can also alter priming directly, and stimulating the standard parietal target changes the subjective side of recollection. Meta-analytic evidence shows that the gains are specific to episodic memory and largest for recollection tests after stimulation before encoding, but the priming contribution to these gains has not been estimated. Conclusions: Process-level claims about stimulation-related memory gains require the priming contribution to be measured. Five measurement steps, centred on matched indirect tests and process-dissociation procedures, make it measurable in the same participants, including in clinical trials.

articles.title: Relating smartphone ‘App-journeys’ to mental health: A novel network analysis approach
articles.authors: Georgia Turner; Maria Concepcion Valdez Gastelum; Ian Axel Anderson; Zelda Brufal; Steven Dillmann; Luisa Fassi; Lukas J. Gunschera; Ivonne Monarca; Oscar Peña Ramirez; Monica Tentori
articles.abstract: Despite substantial concern about how technology use relates to mental health, research attempting to identify beneficial or harmful smartphone activities has yielded mixed results. Here, we show that abstracting away from specific activities, their transition patterns across time relate robustly to user mental health. To quantify this transition structure, we develop a novel network analysis method to capture how each phone user journeys across Apps within a smartphone session. Across two independent datasets, including an exploratory UK sample aged 18-22 (n = 82), and a preregistered replication in the USA aged 15-18 (n = 565, ABCD cohort), we show that ‘App-journey’ networks relate consistently to user mental health. For example, users with higher anxiety symptoms transition to a wider variety of Apps within each phone session (higher network density) and are less likely to confine each session to repeated groups of Apps (lower network modularity). In contrast, we find no relationship between ADHD and network modularity or density, suggesting that App-journey networks may distinguish among different mental health profiles. Additionally, in the exploratory dataset, Apps which users describe as more ‘automatic’ are more central in App-journey networks. In summary, we uncover a relationship between the temporal structure of digital activity and specific mental health symptom categories, which generalizes across samples and age groups. The temporal structure of digital activity may thus represent a hitherto neglected, potentially clinically-relevant dimension of digital behaviour for future research and interventions.

articles.title: Barriers to Bridging Divides in the Real World: A Framework for Addressing Challenges in Affective Polarization Intervention Research
articles.authors: Emily Kubin; Victoria Parker
articles.abstract: Affective polarization is rising across democratic societies, prompting a growing body of research on interventions to reduce partisan animosity. Although these interventions demonstrate promise, their effectiveness often diminishes outside of controlled experimental settings, leaving open questions regarding their durability, scalability, and real-world impact. In this review, we introduce the SCOPE Barriers Framework, highlighting five key challenges facing affective polarization intervention research: Statistical, Cross-disciplinary, Overgeneralization from WEIRD samples, Practical, and Ethical barriers. We argue that these barriers systematically constrain the translation of promising interventions into meaningful societal change. By synthesizing insights across disciplines and evaluating intervention practices through the SCOPE lens, we identify limitations in measurement, generalizability, implementation, and ethical consideration. We conclude by offering recommendations for researchers, practitioners, and institutions to design, evaluate, and deploy interventions that are robust, context-sensitive, and socially responsible. Attending to the SCOPE barriers is essential for advancing polarization research from proof-of-concept to sustained real-world impact.

articles.title: Cognitive Bottlenecks Improve AI Alignment with Human Moral Judgment
articles.authors: Danica Dillion; Debanjan Mondal; Wenlong Zhao; Niket Tandon; Kurt Gray
articles.abstract: As AI becomes increasingly integrated into daily life and high-stakes decision-making, aligning it with human moral judgments is a challenge of profound importance. People often mistrust AI’s moral decisions, partly because its opaque processes differ from human reasoning. We introduce “cognitive bottlenecks” that guide large language models (LLMs) to base moral judgments on a small set of psychologically meaningful features, such as perceived harm, agent intention, and victim vulnerability. Across multiple LLMs and moral frameworks, bottlenecks improved alignment with human moral judgments. Participants viewed bottleneck systems as more moral and trustworthy than systems without bottlenecks, and preferred bottleneck-generated explanations over those produced through standard chain-of-thought prompting. Bottlenecks can be implemented through prompting alone, without model retraining. These findings demonstrate the benefits of integrating psychological theory into AI and offer a scalable approach to improving AI-human alignment.

articles_hidden.title: Toward Sensory Accounts of Autistic Masking: A Perspective
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Poulsen; Melanie Heyworth; Timothy Chan; Diana Weiting Tan
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic masking has typically been understood as the suppression of natural Autistic traits within neuronormative social contexts. However, social interactions are inherently embedded within broader sensory environments, highlighting the need to consider how sensory experiences shape masking processes. Although sensory experiences have been recognized within existing masking research, the sensory dimensions of masking remain comparatively underexplored. In this perspective, we examine sensory masking as an interrelated dimension of broader Autistic masking processes, defined as the conscious or subconscious suppression, inhibition, or override of sensory responses to meet environmental or social expectations. Drawing on recent research and our own lived experience, we describe how these sensory dimensions may emerge developmentally, often as a learned adaptation to unsafe or invalidating experiences. We then consider the cumulative effects of sustained sensory masking. While sensory masking may serve a functional purpose, its chronic and persistent engagement may contribute to burnout and negatively impact well-being and mental health, particularly in the context of prolonged exposure to sensory aversive environments. We also distinguish these sensory dimensions from related processes of sensory self-regulation and sensory unmasking, which involve supporting regulation and reclaiming autonomy through safe sensory self-expression. We conclude by outlining constructive approaches that support sensory safety, self-regulation, and well-being, and propose future research directions to explore the mechanisms, impacts, and potential supports associated with the sensory dimensions of masking.

articles_hidden.title: Computationally efficient interval estimation for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R: A replication of Bauer, Preacher, and Gil (2006)
articles_hidden.authors: Carl F. Falk; Elizabeth Savchenko
articles_hidden.abstract: Bauer, Preacher, and Gil (2006) developed a popular estimation approach for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model, using simulations to evaluate the performance of two computationally efficient ways to obtain intervals for the indirect effect. While the model can be estimated in a variety of software packages, support in R lags behind as the original approaches to interval estimation were demonstrated using commercial software. Recent research with R instead has only demonstrated interval estimation with more computationally intensive methods. Meanwhile, other recent work has focused attention towards how Monte Carlo simulation studies are conducted and reported, highlighting the importance of replicating previous findings. Our goals in this manuscript are twofold. First, we show how to implement the original computationally efficient interval estimation methods for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R. We do so by using the Delta method to obtain elements of the asymptotic covariance matrix among model parameters necessary for these approaches. Second, in a pre-registered study, we evaluate our implementation by attempting to partially replicate the original simulation study by Bauer et al. (2006). In general, our results indicate that our implementation is operating as expected as Type I error rates and coverage were acceptable when assumptions were met. Furthermore, though we observed higher convergence rates, the major findings from Bauer et al. (2006) were replicated. We hope that extensions to this work will help lead to more advanced multilevel mediation analysis models being readily available to applied researchers.

articles_hidden.title: Learning and Using Value Maps in Multi-Dimensional Choice
articles_hidden.authors: Ata Baris Karagoz; Akram Bakkour
articles_hidden.abstract:
When making choices between multi-dimensional options, people draw upon knowledge
of the options’ various properties to make a decision. While much work has probed how
individuals make decisions in these modes, less is known of how learned value maps can
be flexibly composed to support novel decisions. Here we taught participants three separate
perceptual-to-value mappings, each dividing a continuous perceptual dimension into five value
categories. We then had them choose between composite options never encountered during
learning while a mouse-contingent display forced serial information sampling. How the learned
map was read during choice varied widely across people, from fully metric reads (e.g. how
much better) to purely ordinal ones (e.g. which is ahead). We find that ordinal comparison is
not simply a degraded version of the same metric. Instead, participants mix between ordinal
and metric reads. How well each dimension was learned set its weight, while how strongly
learning accuracy depended on the separation between categories lowered both the weights
and the metric share of the read. Both the readout and weights left separable signatures in
information search. Learned value maps are thus composed and then read out to guide choice.

articles_hidden.title: Delusion-like content emerges from common-cause inference over semantically disparate observations
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Schafer; Emmett M. Larsen; Kiyohito Iigaya; Guillermo Horga
articles_hidden.abstract: Delusions are beliefs with extraordinary content, yet computational accounts of delusions have not explained how this content arises. We propose that extraordinary content emerges when an ordinary mechanism, common-cause inference, is applied to semantically disparate observations. We tested this with large language models (LLMs) by systematically manipulating semantic disparity between observations. Single causes inferred by these models from ordinary observations generally resembled true causes, yet became increasingly delusion-like as observations became more disparate. Observation disparity predicted delusionality, and this relationship could be explained geometrically via semantic analogues of common-cause properties. We further tested this idea in a large corpus of real-world delusions. In cases documenting pre-delusional observations, subsequent delusional beliefs were consistent with what LLMs would infer and exhibited corresponding common-cause properties. Together, our findings identify a computational route through which extraordinary delusion-like content can emerge from ordinary causal inference, and demonstrate its relevance to clinical delusions.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond individual features: Identifying computational principles in perceiving visual beauty
articles_hidden.authors: Mustafa Alperen Ekinci; Philipp Flieger; Daniel Kaiser
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research in empirical aesthetics has related beauty to visual features like curvature, color, or shape. Although these feature-based accounts have identified reliable visual correlates of beauty, the literature on feature preferences is highly fragmented, with individual features studied for individual stimulus domains. Here, we argue that making further progress hinges on complementing feature-based approaches with approaches aimed at distilling computational principles that underlie the perception of beauty. Recent advances in computational neuroscience can drive this new line of research by linking visual beauty to the coding of visual information in artificial neural networks and the biological brain. We highlight two examples of how this approach has identified overarching computational principles. First, metabolic processing costs, both in artificial and biological vision, are inversely related to perceived beauty, suggesting that beauty may reflect energy-efficient, fluent visual coding. Second, integrative processing in artificial and biological vision captures the efficient spatial representation of image elements across space and predicts beauty ratings. Synthesizing these findings, we derive a neuro-computational framework for assessing computational principles in the perception of beauty, which uses artificial neural networks for exploration at scale and then validates candidate principles using human behavior and brain data. We discuss candidate principles that could be explored using this approach, like spatiotemporal predictability, and delineate how the new insights could be reconciled with feature-based approaches. In conclusion, complementing feature-based studies with studies targeting computational principles promises a comprehensive and mechanistic understanding of why certain visual stimuli are perceived as beautiful, and others are not.

articles_hidden.title: Team Science: An Examination of Factors Associated with Citation Metrics
articles_hidden.authors: Kelly Cuccolo; Jordan Rose Wagge; John Edlund; Erin Michelle Buchanan
articles_hidden.abstract: Scientific collaboration, often measured through co-authorship, has grown in many disciplines and is frequently linked to increased citation rates. However, it remains unclear which disciplines have seen the greatest growth in collaboration and how this growth relates to article-level metrics. Moreover, little is known about how team demographics (e.g., h-index, gender, number of institutions) and team size interact with regard to research impact. Understanding these dynamics is essential given their influence on hiring, tenure, and the broader scientific ecosystem. Using metadata from Elsevier’s International Center for the Study of Research (ICSR) Lab, we examined collaboration trends across disciplines and their associations with citation outcomes. Team size increased over time, with variation by discipline, and was positively associated with citation counts. Gender relationships with citation rates varied by authorship order and discipline, indicating a complex relationship between gender and impact. Greater institutional and geographic diversity were linked to higher citation counts. Last authors’ h-indices were especially strongly associated with impact, particularly when self-citations were excluded. Effect sizes were small, and the observational design precludes causal conclusions. These findings describe how evolving patterns of collaboration are related to research visibility and underscore the importance of considering team composition, cautiously, in evaluations of scientific output.

articles_hidden.title: Rest-Activity Rhythms, Social Interaction, and Depressive Symptoms in Older Adults: A Longitudinal Within- and Between-Person Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Kyungmi Lee; Jennifer B. Levin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Rest-activity rhythm organization and social interaction have each been linked to late-life depression, yet their independent longitudinal contributions have rarely been examined within a framework separating between-person differences from within-person fluctuations. This study examined their independent associations with depressive symptoms in community-dwelling older adults.
Method: Data from Rounds 12–14 (2022–2024) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) included 1,532 person-wave observations from 606 participants. A Behavioral Rhythm Index (BRI) combined mean activity, relative amplitude, and reversed day-to-day variability. Person-mean-centered random-intercept linear mixed models separated within- from between-person associations, adjusting for wave, age, sex, and education.
Results: Higher BRI was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = −0.238, p < .001) and within persons (B = −0.139, p = .013), although the within-person association was not robust across sensitivity analyses. Greater social interaction was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = −0.714, p < .001) but not within persons. BRI and social interaction did not significantly interact (χ²(2) = 2.05, p = .359).
Conclusion: Higher BRI and greater habitual social engagement were each independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms between individuals, warranting further investigation as potentially modifiable behavioral factors in late-life depression.

articles_hidden.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Geller
articles_hidden.abstract:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

articles_hidden.title: The Emotion Filmmaker: Temporal Memory, Time-Emotion Integration, and Affective Style
articles_hidden.authors: Mengsi Li; Regina C Lapate
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotional experiences are temporally dynamic, but prior work suggests that temporal features are usually neglected in remembered emotion. For instance, retrospective emotion evaluations are often biased by discrete salient timepoints, such as the peak and end moments, at the expense of objective event duration (i.e., peak–end effects and duration neglect). However, how these retrospective emotion biases originate, as well as their significance for emotional functioning, remain unclear. Here, we test the hypothesis that retrospective emotion biases are related to fundamental limits of temporal processing and memory capacity. Further, we examine whether these limits have implications for emotional functioning. Participants (n = 60) underwent a novel paradigm comprising affectively-rich movie sequences while providing emotion ratings continuously (moment-by-moment) and retrospectively. Temporal memory for previously-watched emotional-movie sequences and dispositional negativity were measured. Our findings revealed a greater “end” bias as the duration of emotional-movie sequences increased, suggesting that limitations in temporal processing capacity may contribute to retrospective emotion biases. Critically, temporal-memory errors were associated with larger retrospective emotion biases and with individual differences in dispositional negativity. Collectively, these results indicate that retrospective emotion biases may stem partly from mnemonic temporal errors that are emotionally maladaptive.

articles_hidden.title: The Culture of Dissemblance Among Black American Women: A Mixed Methods Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Linzie Taylor; Natalie Merril; Trinidi Prochaska; Amanda R. Arnold; Amy R Murphy; Megan E. Huibregtse; Angela Li; Abigail Powers; Vasiliki Michopoulos; Jennifer Stevens
articles_hidden.abstract: Disparities in the treatment of mood and stress disorders like posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) may partially reflect a limited culturally informed understanding of emotional processing. The culture of dissemblance (COD) describes how American Black women learned to mask their emotional expression as a protective mechanism within a society that places them at greater risk of psychosocial stressors while invalidating their emotional experience. This mixed methods study examined COD among forty-nine Black women (ages 40–55), who completed a semi-structured interview assessing emotional engagement alongside self-report measures of emotion regulation, trauma exposure, PTSD symptoms, racial discrimination, and Black identity. Thematic analysis indicated that participants experienced negative judgments of their emotional expression and learned to monitor emotional responses for self-protection. 83.7% of women reported less emotional expression in public with 40.8% of women identified the workplace as the primary site for emotional masking. Interview-based COD endorsement associated with belief in negative public perception of Black people but not with the other variables of interests. Treatment approaches should center Black women's cultural knowledge to address mental health disparities.

articles_hidden.title: Does autonomy enhance satisfaction, adherence and clinical outcomes? A Randomized Controlled Trial of a digital mental health intervention for college students
articles_hidden.authors: Sevin Ozmen; Leonore de Wit; Arpana Amarnath; Annemieke van Straten; Sascha Y Struijs
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: College students face high rates of mental health problems including depression and stress. Digital interventions offer accessible support, but adherence remains challenging. Autonomy may enhance motivation, yet its role in student-focused digital interventions is not explored yet in a randomized controlled trial. 
Objective: This study examines whether enhancing autonomy in a guided digital CBT-based mental health intervention for college students (LifeHack) improves satisfaction, adherence, and mental health outcomes.
Methods: In a two-armed randomized trial, 575 students were assigned to either a structured intervention or an autonomy-enhanced version in which participants could select topics of interest. Assessments were conducted at baseline and 5 weeks later (post-intervention). Primary outcomes were general satisfaction (CSQ-8) and working alliance with the program and e-coach (WAI-I); secondary outcomes included adherence, mental well-being (MHC-SF), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and quality of life (MHQoL). 
Results: Participants were moderately satisfied with the intervention and guidance, and showed small-to-moderate improvements in mental well-being, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life from baseline to post-intervention (all p < .001; Cohen’s d ranging 0.24-0.41). However, no significant differences were observed between conditions on satisfaction, adherence or clinical outcomes.
Conclusions: Allowing users to freely choose lesson topics did not enhance satisfaction, adherence, or clinical outcomes compared with a structured lesson sequence. Nonetheless, participation in LifeHack was associated with improved mental health, indicating potential intervention effectiveness regardless of the autonomy features. Future research should test more comprehensive autonomy-supportive designs and compare LifeHack with inactive control conditions to establish intervention effectiveness.

articles_hidden.title: Interindividual Differences in Treatment Effects of a Personality Change Intervention on Life and Domain Satisfaction
articles_hidden.authors: Lara Kroencke; Johannes Zimmermann; Saskia Baumgardt; Lena Brüggmann; Claudia Harzer; Axel Mayer; Mirjam Stieger; Lara Puhlmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality change interventions have shown promising average effects not only on personality traits, but also on well-being. However, little is known about the extent to which these effects differ between individuals and what baseline characteristics are associated with such differences. To answer these questions, we analyzed data from the PEACH intervention, a 10-week smartphone-based personality change intervention (N = 873). Using the EffectLiteR framework for causal inference, we estimated average and individual treatment effects of the intervention (vs. waitlist) on life satisfaction, average life domain satisfaction, and satisfaction with individual domains. Moreover, we tested whether interindividual differences in treatment effects could be predicted by demographic characteristics, baseline personality traits, baseline well-being, motivational factors, and engagement preferences. We found a significant average treatment effect on average domain satisfaction (d = 0.20), concentrated in work- and emotion-related domains, but not life satisfaction. Notably, we identified significant heterogeneity in this effect across participants: For approximately 27% of participants, the PEACH intervention showed positive effects on average domain satisfaction, while for 66% it showed no effects, and for 7% it showed negative effects. Men, individuals rated higher in Openness by observers, and individuals with lower self-reported change goal attainability at baseline benefited most from the intervention. Taken together, these findings suggest that personality change interventions can enhance domain satisfaction for some, but not all, individuals, underscoring the need for personalized approaches and the identification of subgroups for whom interventions may be ineffective or even counterproductive.

articles_hidden.title: The Formation of the Sufferer: Deconstructive Inquiry and the Self-Problem Relation in Psychotherapy
articles_hidden.authors: Arie Todd Greenleaf
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychotherapy generally begins with a person who has a problem and needs help resolving it. Deconstructive Inquiry (DI) examines how the struggle to resolve a difficulty can form the apparent self who must overcome it. This conceptual paper draws on a relational ontology, which understands things as organized patterns of relations. The self who must overcome fear, for example, takes shape through judging, resisting, and trying to escape fear. This activity is experienced as someone separate from the feeling and responsible for ending it. I call this formation centering. Comparison with a remembered past or imagined future can sustain the struggle by making present life unacceptable until the person changes. DI proposes that the effort and its apparent controller can become recognizable as the same activity. The division need not continue, even while fear remains and the person responds to what needs attention. A composite clinical vignette illustrates this possibility and shows how the therapist’s need to prove helpful can reinforce the client’s struggle. I also propose that insight changes the knowledge shaping later encounters, allowing change to persist without requiring the person to recall or repeat the insight. Comparisons with other therapies examine whether a separate observing self remains when therapy succeeds. The paper considers how cultural expectations shape these struggles and how therapists and supervisors can participate in sustaining or questioning them.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing conditionals: An experimental comparison of suppositional and inferential accounts
articles_hidden.authors: Alessandro Bogani; Andrea Iacona; Stefania Pighin; Vincenzo Crupi; Katya Tentori
articles_hidden.abstract: Two main normative accounts have been proposed to explain the acceptability of a conditional. The suppositional account equates acceptability with the probability of the consequent given the antecedent, whereas the inferential account maintains that it depends on the support the antecedent provides to the consequent. Previous empirical work has addressed the descriptive accuracy of normative and non-normative accounts, but the results have been inconclusive. In the present study, we introduce a novel experimental procedure designed to dissociate the predictions of competing accounts and employ it in three experiments. Overall, the results indicate that most individuals endorse a normative interpretation of conditionals; however, the specific account that best captures their judgments depends on the type of conditional evaluated. For conditionals in which the antecedent and the consequent stand in an arbitrary relation (e.g., “If the toy is a triangle, then it will be yellow”), judgments align more closely with the suppositional account. In contrast, for conditionals where the antecedent and the consequent are directly causally related (e.g., “If the laser is misaligned, then the prosthesis will have cracks” or “If the prosthesis has cracks, then the laser was misaligned”), judgments are better captured by the inferential account. Possible extensions of current models aimed at achieving a comprehensive characterization of conditionals are briefly discussed.

articles_hidden.title: The Strengths and Pitfalls of No-report Paradigms in Multistable Perception Research
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel van der Meer; Simon van Gaal; Raoul P P P Grasman; Han L. J. van der Maas; Michael D. Nunez
articles_hidden.abstract: Ambiguous, multistable stimuli can give rise to multiple perceptual interpretations. Bistable visual stimuli, in particular, have long been used to study neurological and cognitive processes. However, many experimental paradigms rely on self-report to assess subjective perceptual experiences, introducing potential issues such as low reliability and interferences of reporting into the processes under investigation. No-report paradigms serve as a method to work around these problems by decoding perceptual content based on physiological data. Here we discuss the strengths and pitfalls of no-report paradigms in the context of research using multistable perception. Focusing on experimental power related to decoding accuracy, we exemplify the current progress of decoding perceptual content using three major domains of physiological data (eye-tracking, M/EEG and fMRI). We find that the predictability of the percept varies significantly depending on the paradigm and stimulus type, showcasing both the potential and limitations of physiological inference in bistable perception research.

articles_hidden.title: Sensory Processing in Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle Luszawski; Caroline Luszawski; Natalie Luszawski; Blake Edward Butler; Bobby Stojanoski; Jason Brown; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a range of developmental differences following the exposure of alcohol in utero. Although not a stand-alone diagnostic criterion for FASD, sensory processing deficits are commonly observed in individuals with FASD. The purpose of this scoping review was to review the existing evidence regarding the sensory processing differences in individuals with FASD compared to neurotypical individuals. A scoping review of the literature was conducted investigating studies of human participants with FASD and neurotypical participants. Studies were included if they reported on sensory processing differences between FASD and neurotypical participants. Any measures of sensory processing and in-utero exposure to alcohol were included. APA Psycinfo, Embase, Medline, Scopus, and CINAHL were searched for relevant studies. A total of 1192 studies were screened for inclusion, of which 42 were extracted. Studies investigated sensory processing differences in unisensory visual, auditory, olfactory, and somatosensory processing, multisensory integration, and sensorimotor processing. Measures of sensory processing included imaging measures (fMRI, MRI), clinical interviews, questionnaires, behavioural tasks, psychometric tests, and electrophysiological measures (EEG, MEG, DTI). Results indicate that differences in sensory processing exist in individuals with FASD when compared to neurotypical controls; however, these differences may vary depending on the age of participants, the type of sensory processing being measured, and other individual participant factors.

articles_hidden.title: Eye See Your Intentions: Age-Related Differences in Gaze Perception and Trustworthiness Attributions
articles_hidden.authors: Alayna Shoenfelt; Reese E. Chadwick; Tian Lin; Sanghee Park; Teodoro Ayub Barres; Natalie C. Ebner
articles_hidden.abstract: Successful social interactions depend on regulating approach-avoidance tendencies as well as accurately understanding those motivations in others. Direct gaze signals approach intentions, whereas averted gaze signals avoidance intentions. Older relative to younger adults display a stronger direct gaze bias (i.e., are more likely to perceive eye gaze as direct vs. averted). This bias in motivational cue perception likely impacts social trait attributions. This study, for the first time, leveraged a lifespan sample across a wide age range (18 – 88 years; N = 307) to investigate adult lifespan differences in gaze perception using a novel set of gaze-modified face stimuli with varying expressions and tested whether perception of gaze aversion affected attributions of facial trustworthiness. Participants were recruited and the study conducted online via Prolific. Faces with more averted gaze were perceived as more direct-looking with age. This bias was relatively weaker for fearful faces compared to all other facial expressions. Further, greater perception of direct gaze was associated with greater facial trustworthiness attributions, and especially with age. Combined, these findings confirm a direct gaze bias in aging and support its impact on social trait attributions. These adult lifespan differences in approach-avoidance motivational cue perception may reflect shifts in sensitivity, capacity, and/or motivation and are discussed as a possible mechanism in greater trust and susceptibility to deception with age. This work also adds substantially to the widely used FACES Lifespan Database corpus by making the newly gaze-modified faces, and their norm ratings, publicly available for research on motivational and cognitive aging.

articles_hidden.title: Methodological Flexibility in the Iowa Gambling Task Undermines Interpretability: A Meta-method Review
articles_hidden.authors: Annika Iris Külpmann; Jan-Paul Ries; Ian Hussey; Malte Elson
articles_hidden.abstract: Methodological flexibility–researcher degrees of freedom in procedure and scoring–can contribute to poor measurement and low replicability of findings. To quantify methodological flexibility in the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT), a widely used measure of decision-making in clinical psychology, we conducted a meta-method review of a random sample of 100 studies. We found prevalent under-reporting and wide-spread modifications of procedural details. We identified 244 distinct scores used to quantify IGT outcomes, 177 of which appeared only once in our sample. To quantify the potential impact of this flexibility, we performed a multiverse analysis using 205 scores on an open IGT dataset. Correlations among these ranged from rs = -0.942 to 0.998 with a median r = 0.022, suggesting that different scoring strategies can produce extremely different study outcomes. Given these findings, without substantive information about which specific procedural and scoring choices were employed, results from the IGT are rendered uninterpretable. Supplementary Materials, Data, and Code are available at github.com/anniria/igt-methodological-flexibility.

articles_hidden.title: Growing Well with Grow It!: Acceptability of a Gamified mHealth App for Adolescents With a Chronic Somatic Illness – A Mixed Methods Study
articles_hidden.authors: Marije van Dalen; Hanneke Scholten; Inge Braspenning; Loes Keijsers; Johanna Wilhelmina Weerdmeester; Jeroen Legerstee; Manon H.J. Hillegers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Over 17% of children live with a chronic somatic illness and are at increased risk of experiencing psychological problems, such as anxiety and depression. Grow It! is a transdiagnostic mobile health (mHealth) intervention that combines experience sampling and personalised mood feedback with daily coping challenges to promote reflection, emotional insight and adaptive coping. The app fosters a collaborative team experience in which participants contribute to growing a shared virtual tree and communicate through a chat function with predesigned stickers. 
Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the acceptability of the Grow It! app among adolescents with a chronic somatic illness and to identify key lessons the development of other gamified mHealth apps designed to promote well-being.
Methods: This preregistered study is part of a randomised waitlist controlled trial. Adolescents with a chronic somatic illness aged 10-18 years old were recruited from a university medical children’s hospital. Upon inclusion, adolescents were randomised to an intervention group that used the Grow It! app or a waitlist control group. Follow up questionnaires were completed immediately after the four week intervention period and three months later. Consecutively, the waitlist control group was also offered the Grow It! app and completed questionnaires immediately after use and three months later. Participants completed user experience survey comprising open ended and closed questions after playing the app. Responses were analysed using qualitative content analysis and descriptive statistics.
Results: Between August 2021 and September 2023, 208 adolescents were included in the study. Due to participant attrition, the user experience survey was distributed to 183 participants and completed by 150 (Mage=13.95, 39.33% male, 59.33% female, 1.33% other). The app received a mean overall rating of 7.32 out of 10, and a mean look-and-feel rating of 7.98 out of 10; 84% would recommend the app to a friend. Participants reported that the app helped them recognise their emotions and gain greater self-insight. They also described its design as colourful and visually appealing. Suggested improvements included adjusting the timing and frequency of the momentary assessments, and expanding the chat function to allow free-text messages or a wider selection of stickers. 
Conclusions: The Grow It! app is well-accepted by adolescents aged 10 to 18 with a chronic somatic illness, although optimising the chat function and reducing questionnaire burden may further improve user experience. Combined with evidence of effectiveness, these findings on acceptability and user experience support the implementation of the Grow It! app in paediatric healthcare.

articles_hidden.title: Analyzing Binary Judgments: An Empirical and Simulation-Based Comparison of Aggregated and Trial-Level Approaches for Hypothesis Testing
articles_hidden.authors: Semih Can Aktepe; Daniel W. Heck
articles_hidden.abstract: Binary judgments are widely used in psychological research to investigate cognitive processes and decision making. Statistical approaches for analyzing such data differ in whether responses are aggregated (e.g., analysis of variance, ANOVA) or modeled at the trial level (e.g., generalized linear mixed models, GLMMs), and in whether results are interpreted as choice proportions or in terms of signal detection theory (SDT) parameters for response bias and discrimination ability. We examined how these approaches differ in specification, interpretation, and results. First, we reanalyzed 20 openly available datasets on the illusory truth effect (212,555 observations), comparing by-subjects (F1) and by-items (F2) ANOVAs of choice proportions, their combination via min-F', a two-step SDT approach (ANOVA of individual SDT estimates), and seven GLMMs with random-effects structures of varying complexity. Second, a Monte Carlo simulation assessed Type I error rates, power, and parameter recovery. GLMMs with random slopes for both participants and items controlled Type I error rates best but often resulted in singular fits. GLMMs with random slopes only for participants were favored by AIC and BIC, but inflated Type I error rates for interactions by ignoring item-specific variability in the repetition effect. Random-intercept-only GLMMs, F1 and F2 ANOVA, and two-step SDT were too liberal for some effects, whereas min-F' was overly conservative. Unlike aggregated analyses, GLMMs account for both participant and item variability and estimate SDT parameters with less bias. We therefore recommend GLMMs with theoretically justified random-effects structure, simplified only if necessary and with the resulting risk of Type I errors for confirmatory hypothesis testing.

articles_hidden.title: A Step-by-Step Tutorial on the Stochastic Cusp Model in R
articles_hidden.authors: Renaud Mabire-Yon; Raoul P P P Grasman; Han L. J. van der Maas
articles_hidden.abstract: People facing similar circumstances may function very differently. The stochastic cusp model offers one possible explanation: the same conditions may support two stable levels of functioning. This tutorial shows how to understand, fit, and interpret the model in R, assuming familiarity with regression and basic R. Simple illustrations explain how stable states emerge and how changing conditions can alter them. A synthetic example links personal resources and acute stress to adaptive functioning. Readers learn to specify the model, check the fit, interpret coefficients and uncertainty, and examine its predictions. At average resources, the fitted distribution changes from one peak at low stress to two separated peaks at higher stress. The tutorial also explains which further observations would help distinguish a cusp hypothesis from competing explanations. Publicly available data, code, and archived output allow readers to reproduce the example.

articles_hidden.title: Bayesian posterior predictive checks for person-fit analysis: A comparison of approaches illustrated with the lz* statistic
articles_hidden.authors: Jorge Tendeiro
articles_hidden.abstract: Person-fit analysis is a popular framework in item response theory aimed at flagging observed response patterns that substantially deviate from a fitted model’s predictions. In this paper we combine and extend previous work by comparing alternative implementations of Bayesian posterior predictive checks for person-fit analysis. Two of the implementations adapt proposals by Berkhof et al. (2004) to person fit for the first time. The suggested procedures are generic and may be used with any person-fit statistic; we use the lz* statistic for illustration purposes. Data-driven empirically calibrated thresholds to use for flagging aberrant response patterns are derived as part of the methodology. Through two simulation studies, we identify two of the considered approaches that generally performed best across varying scenarios of response misfit, one semi-Bayesian and the other fully Bayesian.
