Our simulations further show that the calibrated thresholds for some approaches differ substantially from their nominal threshold counterparts. We illustrate how to use these procedures by means of an empirical example. Our results offer concrete guidance for practitioners conducting person-fit analysis within the Bayesian framework.

articles_hidden.title: Respiratory Phase and Visuospatial Attention: A Replication and Extension
articles_hidden.authors: Timothy Ethan Roberts; Bethanie Richards; Paul Anthony Skarratt; Martin Fischer; Shane Lindsay
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent studies suggest that respiration may influence visuospatial processing. In two experiments, Belli and Fischer (2024) reported faster detection of targets on the right at inhalation peaks and targets on the left at exhalation troughs. We sought to replicate those findings and to test whether the influence of breathing phase on spatial responding would also extend to the vertical dimension. Experiment 1 used a visual probe detection task and Experiment 2 used an exogenous Posner cueing task. Targets appeared at horizontal and vertical locations, with trials manually triggered at visually identified inhalation peaks and exhalation troughs. Across both experiments, the predicted spatial pattern did not emerge on either axis. Experiment 1 yielded no reliable phase effect, whereas Experiment 2 showed shorter reaction times in the inhalation condition than in the exhalation condition across target locations, consistent with a general change in response speed associated with inhalation.

articles_hidden.title: The conflicted student and the internal battle over generative AI use
articles_hidden.authors: Stephen Harrison Dewitt; Metodi Siromahov; Duncan Brumby; Silvia Bodei
articles_hidden.abstract: The common narrative around university students and generative AI is one of crisis. Underpinning this is an implicit assumption: if students have the capacity to cheat, they will. Our survey reveals two missing factors from that narrative: students have ethical principles, and students want to learn. While a minority of students might fit that implicit assumption of the crisis narrative, a similar proportion refuse to use any genAI tools at all. In between these are the majority: students using genAI tools in what they self-define as a ‘supportive’ way. These students, finding these tools unavoidable, worrying about being disadvantaged or simply finding them valuable, struggle to use them in a way that doesn’t compromise their personal sense of authorship, fits with their environmental and social principles, and doesn’t detract from their ability to learn. Students typically care greatly about these issues and are internally conflicted about this, feeling guilt when using these tools and personally trying to find that invisible line where support becomes cheating. They also use a range of rhetorical techniques to frame their personal usage and preserve their sense of authorship. We argue that we need to work with students, using approaches that enhance these feelings and encourage self-discipline, rather than primarily adopting a ‘criminal’ model of checks, detection and punishment.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion Recognition, Face Processing and Crystallized Intelligence in Personality Pathology: A Multimethod Study
articles_hidden.authors: Ludwig Ohse; Emanuel Jauk; Johannes Zimmermann; André Kerber; Leonie Kampe; Jil Mohr; Robert Schierz; Michael Rentrop; Roeland J. Verhallen; Isabel Dziobek
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality disorders (PDs) are commonly associated with impairments in social cognition, particularly emotion recognition. However, evidence also suggests deficits in more basic cognitive functions, including face processing (e.g., detection of non-emotional facial features) and indicators of general intelligence (e.g., crystallized intelligence). We addressed two exploratory research questions: first, how emotion recognition, face processing, and crystallized intelligence relate to personality pathology across categorical and dimensional PD models, and second, whether these associations primarily reflect general or specific personality pathology. We further hypothesized that the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition would be attenuated when controlling for face processing or crystallized intelligence. In a clinical sample (n = 219), cognitive abilities were assessed using performance-based measures, and personality pathology was assessed using interviews and self-reports. Structural equation modeling, including correlated factor and bifactor-(S-1) models, was applied to separate general from specific personality pathology variance. General personality pathology showed strong negative associations with emotion recognition and small-to-moderate negative associations with face processing and crystallized intelligence. Associations with specific personality pathology were substantially attenuated when controlling for general personality pathology. The link between personality functioning and emotion recognition was only minimally accounted for by face processing or crystallized intelligence. These findings suggest that cognitive deficits in PD may primarily reflect severity rather than disorder-specific variance, while the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition appears not to be reducible to face processing or crystallized intelligence. Our study suggests that dimensional models provide a more nuanced framework for understanding cognitive impairment in personality pathology.

articles_hidden.title: Catatonia recovery separates two intervention axes that constrain electroconvulsive therapy
articles_hidden.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles_hidden.abstract: A treatment can start a recovery or carry one further, and outcomes alone do not say whether these are actions on the same quantity. We ask this of a model motivated by catatonia, in which twenty-five inpatients recovered through five capacities in one fixed order and whose two effective treatments have no known dynamical representation. The model is an evidence-coupled bistable cascade on a dependency chain: each capacity is bistable, the threshold falls as evidence consolidates, and recovery propagates from a root by diffusive coupling. Two quantities are taken as intervention coordinates, an excursion applied to the root and the coupling between adjacent capacities, with the evidence coordinate closed to input by assumption; we show that they act on disjoint regions of state space. While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids any non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and in either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so an acute conversion requires an excursion. With the root restored and the downstream chain collapsed, propagation is governed by one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, because the first-stage equilibrium condition factorises; the weakest coupling sets where recovery stops, the same discriminant gives the first-stage eigenvalue and the inverse-square-root passage time through the fold, and the coupling is identifiable from the resting first stage. Eight falsifiable predictions are separated into consequences of the theorems, predictions needing an added clinical correspondence, and predictions needing a latent quantity measured; exploratory comparisons with published data bear on two of them.

articles_hidden.title: Facial Muscle Responses to Child-Related Emotional Stimuli Among Expecting Fathers, First-Time Fathers, and Fathers With Multiple Children
articles_hidden.authors: Sonja Veistola; Marian Bakermans-Kranenburg; Hannah Spencer; Renate S. M. Buisman; Hanneli Sinisalo; Peter Bos; Mikko J. Peltola
articles_hidden.abstract:
Empathy supports effective caregiving, as parents rely on infants’ non-verbal signals to guide their responses. Emerging evidence suggests that men undergo hormonal and neural changes related to empathy during the transition to parenthood. This study investigated men’s empathic reactions towards children by comparing groups at different stages of fatherhood to test a proposal that expecting and first-time fathers show heightened empathic reactivity to children’s distress. With pre-registered analyses, we compared three groups: expecting fathers (N = 35), first-time fathers (N = 44), and fathers of more than one child (N = 39). Participants completed a Picture task and a Video task involving emotional child stimuli. Their facial muscle responses were measured using facial electromyography (zygomaticus and corrugator muscles). Participants also reported their subjective emotional reactions and provided saliva samples for testosterone assessment. Only in the Picture task first-time fathers showed stronger corrugator activity to negative child stimuli when compared with expecting fathers, while self-reported empathy did not differentiate the groups. Testosterone was negatively associated with corrugator responses toward negative pictures of children, but only among expecting fathers. Although group differences were modest, these findings point to subtle shifts in fathers’ responsiveness during the transition to parenthood and indicate that early fatherhood may represent a period of heightened responsiveness to child distress.
Keywords: empathy, fatherhood, emotions, electromyography

articles_hidden.title: Is conscious perception necessary to direct attention? A replication of Jiang et al. (2006): Stage 2 Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Yung-Jung Chen; Ryan Bradley Scott; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: The relationship between attention and consciousness has been debated for decades. Observing attentional biases induced by visual stimuli below the conscious threshold is one way of providing evidence for the independence of attention and conscious perception. Among such studies, Jiang et al. (2006) found a strong priming effect below the objective conscious threshold with high sensitivity, in showing attentional biases to nude images suppressed by continuous flash suppression (CFS). In our replication, we found moderate Bayesian evidence for the unconscious attraction from opposite sex nude images below the subjective conscious threshold in heterosexual participants. This supports the theory that attention and consciousness are dissociable, and the idea that sexually attractive visual stimuli capture attention even when rendered unconscious. The results have been checked for computational reproducibility by an independent statistician, full report at https://osf.io/dr35v/files/te58h.

articles_hidden.title: Transparency for Whom? Participants' Informed Consent in the Era of Open Data
articles_hidden.authors: Michela Zambelli; Rossella Caliciuri; Giulia Moncalieri; Angela Sorgente
articles_hidden.abstract: Open data can extend the use of participants’ information far beyond the study for which it was collected, making informed consent for data sharing an important part of research transparency. We examined whether psychology journals that promote open data address this issue in their guidelines and whether articles sharing data report relevant information about consent. We reviewed the websites of 83 journals identified through the TOP Factor list and examined 196 empirical articles sharing data, published in 2024–2025. No journal provided explicit guidance on obtaining consent specifically for sharing participants’ data on open platforms; four required authors to report consent for secondary data use when applicable. Only seven articles (3.57%) provided information connecting informed consent to data sharing, and in six cases this information was identifiable only in repository materials. These findings reveal a transparency gap: consent for data sharing is rarely made explicit in journal guidance or research reports, even when data are openly shared. We recommend clearer communication with participants about data sharing, more detailed reporting and sharing of consent materials, and stronger guidance from journals and institutions.

articles_hidden.title: Teacher Emotions and Instructional Quality—Insights From the Global  Teaching InSights Video Study: A Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Maximilian Stark; Katrin Lohrmann; Marina Elena Pfeifer; Anne C. Frenzel
articles_hidden.abstract: Existing research into the link between teachers’ emotions and the quality of their lessons has generally relied either on students’ or teachers’ ratings of instructional quality and drawn on teacher samples from homogenous cultural contexts. The present study addressed these limitations by employing data from the multinational Global Teaching InSights study, in which 652 mathematics teachers in eight countries in East Asia, Europe, and South America self-reported their experiences of enjoyment, anger, and anxiety about teaching, and expert raters assessed instructional quality along the three established dimensions of classroom management, socialemotional support, and instructional support. We used fixed-effects linear models to obtain estimates for the covariation between self-reported trait emotions and observer-rated instructional quality dimensions. For social-emotional support, links with teacher anger and teacher anxiety were negative and significant; the link with teacher enjoyment was positive but did not reach statistical significance. These effects were largely homogenous across the international samples, as exploratory analyses revealed. For classroom management and instructional support, effects were negligible in size, and specifically teacher enjoyment–instructional support links were highly internationally heterogeneous. These findings provide essential insights into how teachers’ internal emotional experience translate into their outward instructional behaviors, and the nuances brought about by varying assessment approaches for instructional quality. The observed cross-country variability may spark future cross-national, cross-cultural research in this domain.

articles_hidden.title: A Meta-Analysis of Psychosocial Interventions to Improve Students’ STEM Motivation.
articles_hidden.authors: Jane E Boyle; Geetanjali Basarkod; Johnmarshall Reeve; emily q rosenzweig; Areum Shin; YING MA; Jiesi Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: With global demand for Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) skills increasing, education systems seek to increase student motivation in STEM domains. Psychosocial interventions targeting students’ motivational processes represent a promising approach. This meta-analysis synthesized 289 effect sizes across 38 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine the impact of psychosocial interventions on STEM motivation. Results indicated a small-to-moderate positive overall effect (g = 0.20). Intervention type did not significantly moderate effects, although effect sizes were higher for personal values (g = 0.33), task value (g = 0.18), and framing interventions (g = 0.18). Motivational construct significantly moderated intervention outcomes with effects observed for competence beliefs (g = 0.36), mindset (g = 0.27), and utility value (g = 0.19), while smaller for interest (g = 0.11), and not significant for cost (g = 0.08, p = 0.088) and goals (g = -0.01, p = 0.85). Gender composition significantly moderated intervention effects with greater benefits observed in samples with higher proportions of female students. No significant moderation effects were observed for race, age, educational level, delivery format, country, publication year, peer-review status, or study quality. Qualitative evidence suggested that intervention effects may vary across sociocultural groups, with some indication of stronger responsiveness among first-generation (FG) students and more variable, framing-dependent effects among underrepresented minority (URM) students. These findings imply that psychosocial interventions can enhance STEM motivation when they target competence beliefs, mindset, and utility-value mechanisms, with particularly potential to support groups historically underrepresented in STEM.

articles_hidden.title: A FORAY INTO THE UMWELT OF A PREDATORY BACTERIUM
articles_hidden.authors: Pamela Lyon
articles_hidden.abstract:
The concept of Umwelt refers to the phenomenal world of an organism, defined by its senses
and what it does to stay alive, thrive and reproduce. Umwelt had a powerful influence on how
the scientific study of animal behavior under natural conditions developed in the middle
decades of the 20th century and currently is enjoying renewed interest in the field of
comparative cognition. Traditionally, animals have been the exclusive focus of Umwelt-based
analysis. This chapter focuses on Myxococcus xanthus, a predatory bacterium with an unusual,
complex social lifestyle. The presentation is intended to show that the Umwelt concept can be
useful in unpacking, in radically alien forms of life, processes regarded as cognitive in animals
and in a context (predator–prey interactions) long important to ethology and comparative
psychology, where Umwelt has done most work.

articles_hidden.title: A Comparative Study of Experiential and Distributional Representations for Concrete and Abstract Concepts
articles_hidden.authors: Laxmi R. Iyer; Martin Takac; Igor Farkas
articles_hidden.abstract:
We investigate the semantic distinction between concrete and abstract concepts by
examining the relative contribution of experiential (grounded) features and distributional
(language-based) features in modeling their representation via data driven analysis using
Spearman’s correlation between human similarity ratings, representational similarity
analysis between various feature spaces, multidimensional scaling, and category similarity.
Our results reveal a robust double dissociation between feature types and concept classes.
Grounded features better align with human judgements for concrete concepts than for
abstract concepts. Concrete concepts exhibit higher representational similarity across
different independently obtained grounded feature representations. In contrast, language
based features better align with human judgements for abstract concepts than for concrete
concepts. Abstract concepts exhibit higher representational similarity across different
independently obtained distributional feature representations. Multidimensional scaling
analyses further show that abstract concepts occupy a compressed and highly clustered
region in experiential space, with clustering driven more by degree of abstractness than
semantic similarity. Concrete concepts in contrast are highly correlated with sensorimotor
features in experiential space. Further, better category similarity for concrete concepts is
exhibited by experiential features rather than distributional features.

articles_hidden.title: Young Children’s Help-Seeking Expectations in Teacher-Child Interactions:  The Effects of Teachers’ Familiarity and Response Valence
articles_hidden.authors: Yilun Zhao; YUAN SHEN; Tianxin Song; Wenshuo Li; Ke Shen; anonymous; Jinliang Qin
articles_hidden.abstract: Effective help-seeking is essential for young children’s adaptation in early childhood education settings, yet little is known about how they selectively seek help based on different social cues. This study examined how young children integrate teachers’ familiarity and response valence when predicting a protagonist’s help-seeking behavior. Across two studies, 90 Han Chinese children aged 4–6 years (45 boys) completed a third-party task simulating teacher-child interactions. In Study 1, familiarity was manipulated using photographs of each child’s real teachers, whereas Study 2 employed standardized cartoon figures and verbal cues to indicate familiarity. The results showed that children tended to expect that the protagonist would seek help from familiar teachers, especially those who responded positively. Meanwhile, they hesitated to expect that the protagonist would seek help from unfamiliar teachers, regardless of their response valence. This pattern indicates that familiarity consistently exerted a stronger influence than response valence, as children consistently prioritized familiarity when anticipating support. Together, these findings highlight how young children flexibly integrate multiple social cues when forming help-seeking expectations and offer practical implications for fostering secure, responsive teacher-child relationships in early education.

articles_hidden.title: Whisper automatic speech recognition and humans are similarly sensitive to accents, but use sentence context differently
articles_hidden.authors: Junrong Chen; Jan Kwong; Sarah Paull; Sarah Creel
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite advancements in speech recognition technology, questions remain about model generalizability and how much models mirror human comprehension. These questions are addressed by comparing OpenAI's Whisper model and 75 human transcribers on 300 English sentences (20 speakers, half F, half M, half US-accented, half Spanish-accented). Sentences ended in 100 target words: 1⁄3 high-predictability sentences (The farmer milked the cows), 1⁄3 low- predictability (The farmer milked the nose), and 1⁄3 low-predictability+nonword (The marmer milked the nose). Target word transcription error rates were examined both in sentences and in isolation (recordings excised from same sentences). Errors decreased with increasing model size, but remained heightened for Spanish-accented vs. US-accented speech, roughly similar to human transcribers. Both models and humans benefited from higher sentence predictability. However, sentence context affected models and humans differently: humans benefited only from high- predictability sentences, while models benefited from any sentence context. Humans numerically outperformed the (best-performing) large model on isolated words and showed different error patterns, suggesting Whisper may have a restricted distribution of short utterances or may need lengthier acoustic context than humans. More varied training data and better context awareness, including speaker identity and pragmatic context, might improve ASR generalization.

articles_hidden.title: The Animal Affective Picture System (AAPS):  A Standardized 800-Picture Database for Cuteness and Kawaii Study
articles_hidden.authors: Hiroshi Nittono; Nonoka Nakamura
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological and neuroscientific research on emotions requires publicly available stimulus materials with normative ratings. However, the necessary rating values for certain dimensions may be lacking when conducting research for specific purposes. In this study, we developed a new affective picture collection, the Animal Affective Picture System (AAPS, pronounced ay-apps), intended for use in research on cuteness or kawaii in Japanese and on human–animal relationships. While cuteness is considered a stimulus attribute with positive valence, kawaii also refers to the feeling people experience when perceiving cuteness. A total of 800 animal images in the public domain or licensed under CC0 (1,000 x 1,000 pixels) were rated by 914 Japanese adults on a 9-point scale for four dimensions: valence, arousal, motivational direction (approach–avoidance), and cuteness/kawaii. Each image was rated by an average of 57 participants. Cuteness ratings were highly correlated with both valence and motivational direction (rs = .97), and the positive correlation remained moderate even when one variable was partialed out (rs = .62 and .64, respectively). These results support the idea that kawaii is a positive emotion associated with approach motivation. The AAPS images, mean rating values, and raw data are freely available for download.

articles_hidden.title: Do I experience anxiety, anger, and happiness in the same way as you do? A relational approach to emotion qualia across levels of alexithymia
articles_hidden.authors: Lin Lipeng; Zhang Chuyin; Naotsugu Tsuchiya
articles_hidden.abstract: Do people experience emotions in the same way? How can we characterize the sameness of emotional quality? Qualitative aspects of emotional experience are usually communicated through words. However, words can be ambiguous and can mean different things to different people. Here, we introduce a relational approach, which minimizes the reliance on language yet characterizes emotional experiences as structure, based on similarity judgments among emotion-evoking videos. This Registered Report will apply this method to characterize a psychological condition of “alexithymia,” which is described as “no words for emotions”. In two experiments, participants will rate the similarity between successive videos, based on the feelings evoked by the videos. Repeated video pairs will measure the degree of consistency in their similarity judgments. We will test whether individuals scoring high and low in alexithymia differ in the structure and consistency of their judgments. To disentangle the structures driven by sensory, rather than emotional, aspects of the videos, we will run a control experiment where participants rate the similarity of videos, ignoring the evoked emotions. A pilot study (N = 679) supports the feasibility of this design. By bypassing verbal reports, our approach can inform the study of emotional experience and help to clarify the nature of alexithymia.

articles_hidden.title: Age-of-acquisition Effects across the Adult Lifespan: Evidence from Eye Movements in Compound Word Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; wanyin li; Meyrem Tompson; Kevin Paterson
articles_hidden.abstract: The Age of Acquisition (AoA) effect is where words acquired during childhood are recognised more quickly than those acquired during adulthood. However, the influence of AoA on compound words and its stability across the adult lifespan remain under-investigated. We conducted two eye-tracking experiments to clarify how the AoA effect is moderated by ageing and spacing. Ninety British English adults participated across two eye-tracking experiments: 60 young adults (30 reading unspaced compounds in Experiment 1 and 30 reading spaced compounds in Experiment 2) and 30 older adults (who read both unspaced and spaced compounds across experiments). Using Bayesian linear mixed-effects models, we observed a robust AoA effect in both spaced and unspaced compound words in young adults. However, in older adults, we only observed an AoA effect in unspaced compound words. The AoA effect declined with increasing age, whereas the slope of AoA effect was shallower in spaced than unspaced compound words. These findings suggest that the functional influence of AoA is contingent upon orthographic structure and reading experience: while whole-word AoA influences processing across visual formats in younger readers, older readers shift away from whole-word lexical properties toward constituent-level strategies when orthographic structure is disrupted by spacing.

articles_hidden.title: Economic Evaluations of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca L. Acabchuk; Nana Amma O.O. Larbi; Patricia M. Herman; Vinicius Vieira Vieira Neves; Simon Goldberg; Shufang Sun; Laura N Haygood; Regan Gregory; Blair T. Johnson; Loucks B Eric
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
As healthcare systems increasingly emphasize value-based care, evidence regarding the economic implications of nonpharmacologic interventions is needed to inform implementation and reimbursement decisions. This study aimed to assess the economic value of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, identify clinical populations in which economic evaluations have been conducted, and assess the strength of the available economic evidence.

Design
Systematic review of economic evaluations.

Setting and Participants
All clinical populations and healthcare settings. 

Interventions
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR).

Evidence Review Methods
This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses 2020 guidelines and was prospectively registered. Nine databases, including MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus, were searched from inception through March 2026 without language restriction, with reference-list screening and citation tracking. Eligible studies evaluated Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction and at least one economic outcome. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed quality using the Quality of Health Economic Studies instrument and the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards 2022 checklist.

Results
Among 468 identified records, 12 economic evaluations met inclusion criteria. Studies included 8 randomized clinical trials, 2 Markov models, and 2 prospective cohort studies, conducted in North America (6) and Europe (6). Chronic pain conditions were most frequent (6), followed by mental health disorders (3), breast cancer survivorship (2), and pulmonary arterial hypertension (1). Across these populations, reductions in healthcare utilization and productivity losses generally offset delivery costs, resulting in lower overall costs with equivalent or improved health outcomes for Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction compared with treatment-as-usual. Results were also favorable or comparable relative to active comparators including cognitive behavioral therapy. Despite intervention costs of $195 to $866 per participant (mean, $461), all cost-utility analyses comparing Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction with treatment-as-usual over at least 6 months reported lower costs with equivalent or improved outcomes. Methodological quality was high, with 10 of 12 studies meeting above 80% quality criteria and 5 achieving 100% adherence. Reporting transparency was generally strong.

Conclusions
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction was associated with favorable economic outcomes across chronic pain, mental health, and breast cancer survivorship populations. Current evidence suggests that MBSR may represent a high-value nonpharmacologic intervention, with reductions in healthcare utilization and productivity losses frequently offsetting intervention costs. Additional economic evaluations are needed in underrepresented populations, healthcare settings, and delivery models.

articles_hidden.title: Specifying Innateness in Infant Development: A Framework for Theory-Building Based on Co-Determination
articles_hidden.authors: Leher Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Infant research has often treated early neural and behavioral expression as a privileged window into the initial state of the mind, with early-emerging capacities sometimes uncritically taken as evidence of innate knowledge. This paper evaluates the strength of such inferences through four intersecting lenses: genetics and epigenetics, cultural evolution, definitional precision, and standards of scientific explanation and falsifiability. It distinguishes among several non-equivalent forms of innateness, including claims about representational content, architectural or processing biases, developmental canalization, and maturational timing. In place of broad or underspecified appeals to innateness, it advances co-determination as a framework for theory-building that encourages specification of the biological constraints, experiential inputs, cultural ecologies, developmental timing, and interactive mechanisms proposed to produce a given outcome, as well as the patterns of variation that would support or challenge those claims. The central aim is to provide a more precise and testable basis for theorizing about the initial state of the infant mind.

articles_hidden.title: A Structured Framework for Cumulative Research Reporting in Psychology: Integrating Replication, Effect Sizes, and Meta-Analytic Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolás Sánchez-Álvarez
articles_hidden.abstract: The accumulation of scientific knowledge in psychology is often impeded by the predominance of isolated empirical studies that rarely integrate their findings quantitatively with prior evidence. This limitation contributes to fragmented knowledge bases, inconsistent effect size estimates, and reduced cumulative scientific progress. The present article proposes and formalizes a Cumulative Integrated Reporting (CIR) framework, a structured methodology for empirical reporting designed to improve the systematic integration of new findings within the existing body of literature. The CIR framework consists of four interconnected components: (a) mandatory reporting of effect sizes with appropriate uncertainty estimates, (b) formal comparison with effect sizes from prior studies and relevant meta-analyses, (c) Bayesian-compatible updating of cumulative evidence distributions, and (d) transparent documentation of methodological moderators that could account for cross-study heterogeneity. We illustrate the framework with an applied example using the association between emotional regulation and perceived stress, demonstrating how a single observed effect (r = -.34) can be meaningfully situated within a prior distribution of cumulative evidence. We discuss implications for journal reporting standards, graduate training, and the reformulation of replication as a continuous epistemic practice rather than a discrete binary event. The CIR framework represents a methodologically tractable and practically implementable step toward transforming psychology's reporting culture from one oriented toward confirmatory hypothesis testing to one oriented toward cumulative quantitative synthesis.

articles_hidden.title: Development of Chest X-Ray Interpretation Skills in Trainee Radiologists: Changes in Detection Accuracy and Visual Search Behaviour Following a Two-Day Training Course
articles_hidden.authors: Kayley Birch-Hurst; Hannah Abromowitz; Sanjay Anton Ajithraj; Maahi Padda; Keira Smith; Nieves Vallejo Gaspar; James Hall; Kieran G. Foley; Phillip Wardle; Kait Clark
articles_hidden.abstract: Detecting and interpreting abnormalities in chest X-rays (CXR) is a complex visual search task. Differences between novice and expert performance in medical image perception are well documented but less is known about how early training shapes trainees’ detection accuracy, error types, and gaze patterns. Novices are often taught systematic viewing strategies, yet these may be ineffective without sufficient knowledge of normal variants and pathological appearances. Educational interventions aim to improve knowledge and recognition of normal and abnormal features, but their impact on scanning behavior and error taxonomy has rarely been examined. The present study examined the early development of CXR interpretation skills by assessing changes in detection accuracy and visual search behaviour following a two-day training course. To this end, first-year radiology trainees completed a CXR detection task while their eye movements were recorded before and after training. Images varied in difficulty, including cases with single obvious or subtle abnormalities and cases with multiple findings. Trainees showed modest improvements in detecting abnormalities and near-ceiling performance for cases with obvious findings. However, false-positive rates persisted on over 60% of abnormal cases and over a third of normal cases, and error rates for subtle- and multiple-abnormality cases still exceeded 70% after training. Most errors arose when trainees fixated abnormalities but did not mark them as abnormal, suggestive of faulty decision-making rather than inadequate scanning or failure to recognize suspicious regions. These findings suggest that early CXR training should prioritize strengthening discrimination of subtle pathology through perceptual learning and calibration of decision thresholds.

articles_hidden.title: The effects of oral versus written knowledge task prompt delivery in medical device usability testing
articles_hidden.authors: Anders Orn; Logan T Markwell
articles_hidden.abstract: Knowledge tasks (KTs) are commonly used in medical device human factors (HF) testing to assess participant understanding that cannot be evaluated through direct observation. However, it is unclear whether presenting KTs orally or in writing influences participant behavior or task performance. This study compared oral and written KT prompt presentation in 38 lay adults who each completed 10 KTs for two consumer medical devices. Participants responded verbally in both groups and had access to the device instructions for use (IFU). The Written KT delivery resulted in statistically higher accuracy than the Oral delivery for the blood pressure monitor (65% vs. 47%) and nebulizer (85% vs. 72%), as well as greater frequency of IFU consultation (64% vs. 32% and 65% vs. 36%, respectively). The Written KT Group also had longer pre-response and total task times and fewer moderator interventions, whereas response duration did not differ between groups. To our knowledge, this is the first study to directly examine KT prompt delivery in medical device HF testing. The findings indicate that oral and written KT prompts may lead to different results and participant behavior. Accordingly, whether KT prompts are presented orally or in writing should be treated as a deliberate study design choice, standardized within studies, and clearly reported.

articles_hidden.title: No Memory Needed? Perceptual Matching Accounts for a Large Part of the Working Memory–Intelligence Link
articles_hidden.authors: Gidon T. Frischkorn; Klaus Oberauer; Alessandra S. Souza
articles_hidden.abstract: Working memory capacity (WMC) and fluid intelligence (Gf) are strongly correlated, usually attributed to shared demands on WM maintenance. We test this account against an alternative: shared representational quality. We included an experimentally controlled simplification of visual WM tasks – a perceptual matching task without maintenance demands – alongside WMC and Gf measures. Study 1 (N = 346; younger and older adults) used color and orientation stimuli; Study 2 (N = 267; younger adults) added luminance matching and a broader WMC battery. Matching accuracy strongly predicted Gf and accounted for a large share of the WMC–Gf covariance. WM maintenance accounted for unique Gf variance over and above matching in all groups. These findings are consistent with a shared signal-to-noise ratio affecting perceptual discrimination, WMC, and Gf. They question the view that the WMC–Gf relationship reflects only demands on WM maintenance, while confirming a specific role of maintenance for Gf.

articles_hidden.title: Perfectionism and Excellencism in Parents of Teenagers in Organized Sports: The Place of the Child in the Parent’s Self-Concept
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas L. D. Boivin; Benjamin J. I. Schellenberg; Patrick Gaudreau
articles_hidden.abstract: Parents of children in organized sports have become increasingly involved in their children’s sport journeys and there are growing concerns about their behaviors when attending their children’s competitions. One potential driver of these negative behaviors is the inclusion of the child in the parent’s self-concept. In this study, based on the Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP), we examined if levels of excellencism and perfectionism in sports parents were associated with different indices of parental investment in a child’s sport, including the inclusion of the child and their child’s sport in the self-concept, child-invested contingent self-esteem, self-based pride, and social comparison-based pride. We recruited 330 parents with a teenager participating in organized sports (Mparents = 43.28 years old; SDparents = 6.48 years). Results of a confirmatory factor analysis supported the two-factor structure of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) with parents. Results of multiple regression showed that excellencism positively predicted identification with the child, child-invested contingent self-esteem, self-based pride, and social comparison-based pride. In contrast, perfectionistic standards were positively associated with inclusion of the child in the self-concept, inclusion of the sport of the child, and child-invested contingent self-esteem, while negatively predicting self-based pride. In all, perfection strivers are more identity invested in their child’s sport journey compared to excellence strivers. Overall, the results of the study supported our hypothesis that perfection strivers are at a higher risk of overidentifying with their children who compete in youth sports.

articles_hidden.title: Mehr als Expo: Expositionstherapiegeneralisierung
articles_hidden.authors: Jan Heistermann; Armin Zlomuzica
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Exposure therapy (expo) is regarded as one of the most effective treatments for mental health conditions characterized through anxiety symptomatology. Its effectiveness was repeatedly demonstrated. However, it remains elusive how expo effects generalize and how an expo tailored to specific anxiety symptoms affects comorbidities. Research Question. What is the current state of research on generalization of exposure-based effects (exposure therapy generalization; ETG)? Can exposure-induced effects translate to other contexts, stimuli and comorbidities? Which factors and conditions account for ETG? Materials and Methods. To answer these questions, the present review was conducted to sight and summarize the empirical studies and reviews on ETG. The findings were embedded regarding routine care. Results. Successful expo treatment with specific stimuli and situations may lead to improvements in handling perceptually, thematically or conceptually similar fear stimuli and situations that were left untreated. Results on transdiagnostic therapy indicate that next to specific anxiety symptoms, expo can tackle comorbidities by targeting underlying factors. Disgust appears to be more persistent against ETG. Conclusion. Beneficial exposure-based effects go beyond the treated stimulus and can generalize to non-treated fears and comorbidities. Core implications of these findings for routine care and future research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: The relationship between implicit and explicit stigma of mental illness among mental health clinicians: a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher Jones; Eleftherios Kipoulas; Emma Černis; Peter Beazley
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mental health clinicians have been found to demonstrate stigma towards people with
mental illness through both implicit and explicit methodologies. These are thought to represent
distinct yet potentially related dimensions of stigma. However, the association between implicit and
explicit stigma is unclear, limiting our understanding of how these could impact clinical outcomes.

Aim: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesise research on the relation between
implicit and explicit stigma among mental health clinicians and examine its potential moderators.

Methods: The protocol was preregistered on PROSPERO (CRD42024614725). A systematic search
was conducted using PsycINFO, PsycArticles, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ProQuest Central, Web of
Science, CINAHL, and Scopus. A random-effects meta-analysis of r-to-z transformed correlations
was conducted along with tests of heterogeneity, moderators and publication bias. The features of
implicit and explicit measures, methodological quality and clinical outcomes were also extracted.

Results: Ten studies (n = 1,404 clinicians) with 11 independent samples were included. There was a
statistically significant, but small, positive pooled correlation between implicit and explicit stigma
measures (r = 0.13; 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.23). Heterogeneity was moderate and largely accounted for by
studies examining substance use disorder, which showed a slightly stronger correlation (r = 0.27)
than for other psychiatric disorders (r = 0.08). Publication bias was not detected.

Conclusions: Implicit and explicit stigma appear to be weakly related, so could be considered largely
distinct constructs among clinicians. Findings underscore the importance of addressing implicit and
explicit stigma in research and practice, which may inform stigma-reduction efforts.

articles_hidden.title: Rationally Selected Utility – A New Theory of Riskless Choice
articles_hidden.authors: Shreya Sinha; Agnieszka Tymula; Paul Glimcher
articles_hidden.abstract: Traditional prescriptive decision theories from Pascal’s Expected Value to Expected Utility have struggled to explain inconsistent human choices, leading to purely descriptive models like prospect theory. This paper introduces a novel approach to understand why these behaviors occur, reconciling these observed irrationalities with a simple rational objective, specifically in the domain of riskless choice when choosing between options with certain outcomes. Here, we propose that the human nervous system, faced with limited cognitive capacity (a finite representational precision for the subjective values of rewards), optimally selects a task-appropriate utility function to either maximize long-run average earnings or to minimize errors when choosing between certain outcomes. We argue that the utility functions psychologists and economists have measured empirically are tools, sculpted by knowledge of the choice environment's probabilistic structure and the decision-maker's precision level, for optimally achieving a rational objective. Our results show that almost every experimentally observed utility function can be described as a near-optimal tool for achieving a maximization of objective earnings, a goal abandoned since Bernoulli. We quantify the specific gains that result when a chooser decides to add more cognitive capacity when facing a choice and find that these gains are quite small as long as the utility function is rationally selected. Our research provides a novel framework that offers a testable and foundational explanation for why human and animal decision-makers evolved the puzzling range of utility functions and risk attitudes that have been observed empirically.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Biliteracy and Bidirectional Cross-Linguistic Transfer in a Low Literacy and Multilingual Context: Insights from Internally Displaced Children in Northeast Nigeria
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Akkad; Ashley Wong Ke Wei; Mary-Claire Ball; Sharon Wolf; Kaja Kinga Jasińska
articles_hidden.abstract: Internally-displaced children often lack schooling and reside in highly multilingual contexts. In Nigeria, children must learn to read in a local language (e.g., Hausa), and English; here, language skills can transfer across languages to support biliteracy. Importantly, the strength of transfer is constrained by proficiency in language skills. Formal schooling and early life exposure are crucial for acquisition of language skills. In our sample of 1595 Nigerian internally-displaced children, we investigated how pre-displacement school enrollment and early life language language exposure (i.e., at home) predict language skills, and how language skills transfer across languages to support literacy. Pre-displacement school enrollment particularly supported phonological awareness, and early life language exposure particularly supported vocabulary. Phonological awareness was stronger in Hausa relative to English, resulting in greater transfer from Hausa to English. IDP context allows the investigation of cognition and environment to enrich theoretical models of biliteracy, and inform pedagogical practices.

articles_hidden.title: Bayes Factors for Structural Equation Models with Blavaan and Bridge Sampling
articles_hidden.authors: Julius M. Pfadt; Edgar C. Merkle; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers
articles_hidden.abstract: Bayes factors offer a graded measure of statistical evidence that is increasingly popular in experimental psychology. In the field of structural equation modeling (SEM), however, computational and conceptual challenges have frustrated the broader adoption of Bayes factors. We present a practical Bayes factor workflow that uses bridge sampling to estimate marginal likelihoods for models specified in standard SEM syntax. The workflow starts from a unit-information (UI) prior derived from maximum-likelihood fits, providing a Bayesian analogue of the BIC. We then show how targeted prior variants for focal structural relations may alter and often sharpen the evidence, particularly when directional information is taken into account. A simulation study demonstrates that bridge-sampled UI Bayes factors closely track the BIC approximation and that correct directional prior information substantially increases support for the data-generating model. An empirical dataset is used to showcase two specific extensions, namely (a) robust mixture priors, and (b) Bayesian model averaging. The model averaging integrates across structurally different models and across different prior distributions for the model parameters. The proposed Bayes factor workflow is intended to make Bayesian model comparison in SEM feasible, transparent, and extensible.

articles_hidden.title: Study protocol for a randomised controlled trial of the BODYPOSI digital body image intervention for improving body image among postpartum women
articles_hidden.authors: Gabija Jarašiūnaite-Fedosejeva; Erika Gibė; Gabija Juzėnaitė; Viktorija Stankevičienė; Eglė Urvelytė; Burcu Kömürcü Akik; Amera Mojahed
articles_hidden.abstract: The high prevalence of body image concerns during the transition to motherhood underscores the need for theory-driven, accessible interventions that promote positive body image, reduce body dissatisfaction, and enhance women's resilience to unrealistic appearance ideals. This paper presents the protocol for a two-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating the effectiveness of BODYPOSI, a four-week digital self-help program based on positive body image theory. The trial will include women between 6 weeks and 12 months postpartum, who will be randomly assigned to either the intervention or a waitlist control group. Primary outcomes will include body appreciation, body functionality appreciation, appearance and weight satisfaction, evaluation of postpartum body changes, and perceived sociocultural appearance pressure related to postpartum body changes. Secondary outcomes will include postnatal depressive and anxiety symptoms, self-compassion, and general health status. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and three-month follow-up. Analyses will compare changes between the intervention and control groups and examine the maintenance of intervention effects at follow-up for intervention group. If shown to be effective, BODYPOSI has the potential to improve body image and psychological well-being among postpartum women while supporting the wider implementation of accessible digital interventions in postpartum care.

articles_hidden.title: Which memory does brain stimulation improve? The priming problem
articles_hidden.authors: Halil Aziz Velioglu; murat can çelik; Dogukan Aslan; Mehmet Akif Sakiroglu; Yusuf Çiçek; Ali Tarik Altunc
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of cortical sites connected with the hippocampus improves scores on episodic memory tests and is being tested for memory decline, including in Alzheimer's disease. These gains are read as gains in intentional retrieval. Objective: To examine whether standard memory outcomes can support this reading and how the contribution of repetition priming can be measured. Methods: Narrative review of hippocampal-network stimulation studies, cognitive and electrophysiological research on priming and processing fluency, stimulation studies of priming and parietal cortex, and clinical trials of TMS for memory decline. Results: Old/new recognition and cued recall present studied items or cues again at test. Repetition priming makes these items easier to process, and this fluency can raise a memory score with intentional retrieval unchanged. The fluency behind word-recognition decisions is largely conceptual, so it persists after a change of surface form. TMS can also alter priming directly, and stimulating the standard parietal target changes the subjective side of recollection. Meta-analytic evidence shows that the gains are specific to episodic memory and largest for recollection tests after stimulation before encoding, but the priming contribution to these gains has not been estimated. Conclusions: Process-level claims about stimulation-related memory gains require the priming contribution to be measured. Five measurement steps, centred on matched indirect tests and process-dissociation procedures, make it measurable in the same participants, including in clinical trials.

articles_hidden.title: Rhythm of Thought: Tracing the Dynamics of Deliberation in Reasoning
articles_hidden.authors: Jérémie Beucler; Wim De Neys
articles_hidden.abstract: When an intuitive answer is uncertain, people are thought to reason further. But what people do during this additional thinking, how it unfolds over time, and why it sometimes helps remain unclear. We scored think-aloud protocols with large language models to track, moment by moment, four functions of deliberation (generating candidate responses, justifying them, controlling intuitive responses, and regulating cognitive effort) and expressed confidence. Deliberation showed a temporal organization: generation dominated early, whereas justification, control, and regulation grew as reasoning progressed. Correct responses involved more justification, control, and regulation than biased responses, and these dynamics predicted accuracy for out-of-sample participants and items. Confidence and deliberation showed reciprocal lagged associations: lower confidence predicted further generation, justification, and control, whereas regulation predicted increases in confidence. Deliberation, then, appears to involve not a single act of “thinking harder,” but an evolving interplay of reasoning processes whose organization is linked to whether reasoning succeeds.

articles_hidden.title: Experiencing Pain, Seeking Care, and Being Believed: A Qualitative Study of Autistic Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Stefen Beeler-Duden; Emma H. Baker; Emily A. Hickey; Katiana Estrada; Kevin Pelphrey
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Understanding pain in autistic adults necessitates careful consideration of how pain is experienced, communicated, and interpreted by others. The present study investigated autistic adults' perspectives on pain, healthcare-seeking decisions, and the consequences of pain in daily life.

Methods: Seventy-four autistic adults responded to three open-ended survey questions regarding their pain experiences, interactions with healthcare professionals, and the consequences of pain. Responses were analyzed using inductive qualitative content analysis, followed by higher-order synthesis of categories across questions. Frequencies of coded categories and themes were calculated descriptively.

Results: Four higher-order themes were identified: Approaches to Healthcare Engagement (74.3%), Disruption of Functioning (41.9%), Pain Perception and Experience (37.8%), and Communicating and Being Believed (33.8%). Participants reported variability in pain characteristics and awareness, difficulties articulating pain, concerns regarding whether others recognized or believed their experiences, and effects on daily activities and emotional well-being. Half of the participants reported delaying conventional medical care without pursuing an alternative. Accounts of healthcare engagement included distrust and fear of dismissal, as well as self-advocacy and independent pain management.

Conclusion: Autistic adults' accounts highlight the importance of distinguishing between difficulties in recognizing or communicating pain and difficulties in having pain understood or believed by others. Pain assessment should account for individual differences in pain experience, as well as the interpersonal and healthcare contexts in which pain is interpreted. Incorporating autistic adults' perspectives may facilitate more individualized and responsive care.

articles_hidden.title: Modulating factors of the episodic–semantic continuum in autobiographical memory
articles_hidden.authors: Silvy Collin; Heja Yakut
articles_hidden.abstract: The distinction between episodic and semantic memory has long been central to theories of autobiographical recall, yet accumulating evidence suggests that this boundary is empirically less clear-cut. Autobiographical remembering is increasingly understood as a constructive process in which episodic and semantic components are dynamically integrated rather than retrieved in isolation. In this review, we adopt the theoretical stance that the relative weighting of episodic and semantic information during recall is flexibly modulated by multiple factors, including age, task demands, temporal distance, emotional salience, and communicative goals. We synthesize findings demonstrating how these factors bias recall toward more episodic or more semantic representations and examine how they interact with one another and with situational context. By outlining these modulating influences, the review aims to better understand the mechanics of the episodic-semantic continuum during autobiographical recall and to clarify implications for how autobiographical memory is studied and interpreted across contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring the Relation Between Spatial Anxiety and Mathematics: Spatial Skills, Math Anxiety, and the Unbounded Number Line
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Ayesu; Darcy Hallett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Spatial skills are consistently associated with mathematical performance, and numerical magnitude representation may partially explain
this relationship. However, it remains unclear whether spatial anxiety is similarly associated with mathematics. We sampled
221 adults and assessed spatial skills, spatial anxiety, unbounded number line estimation, math anxiety, and mathematical performance.
Spatial skills were assessed using mental rotation and surface development tasks, while spatial anxiety and math anxiety
were measured with self-report scales. We evaluated numerical magnitude knowledge using an unbounded number line estimation
task, and we measured mathematical performance across arithmetic, fractions, algebra, and percentages. Higher spatial anxiety
was associated with poorer spatial skills and lower mathematical performance. Moreover, spatial skills accounted for part of the
association between spatial anxiety and mathematics, whereas unbounded number line estimation did not, even after controlling
for math anxiety. These findings suggest that spatial anxiety may be associated with poorer mathematical performance without a
corresponding association with numerical magnitude knowledge as measured by unbounded number line estimation. The results
highlight potential differences in the cognitive operations underlying spatial skills and spatial anxiety in relation to mathematics.

articles_hidden.title: From Data to Dialogue: Using Person-Specific Networks to Personalize Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment for Chronic Pain
articles_hidden.authors: Saskia Scholten; Verena Eunike Hofmann; Felicitas Kininger; Julia Glombiewski
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Person-specific network models are increasingly proposed for identifying optimal treatment targets, but how they function in clinical decision-making remains largely unknown. This proof-of-concept study integrated ecological momentary assessment (EMA), person-specific networks, and modular evidence-based interventions in the treatment of chronic pain and examined feasibility, preliminary effects, and acceptability.
Method: Twelve patients completed treatment with one of nine therapists. An intensive EMA phase (six prompts daily for three weeks) informed network-based module recommendations, which were compared with independent clinical judgment. Subsequent phases were monitored three times weekly and analyzed in a single-case experimental design with randomized baselines. Patients and therapists were interviewed after treatment.
Results: Participants provided a mean of 298 observations; seven of 12 met the 80% compliance criterion in all phases. Network-based recommendations largely diverged from clinical judgment. Disability decreased on average (b = -0.45, p = .03), but individual effects were mixed, with no significant baseline-corrected Tau and two participants deteriorating. Patients and therapists primarily valued self-monitoring and structured, data-informed reflection, which increased awareness of everyday patterns and structured the therapeutic dialogue.
Conclusions: The clinical value of data-informed personalization may lie less in algorithmic precision than in facilitating patient-centered, reflective clinical reasoning.

articles_hidden.title: Teacher Emotions and Instructional Quality—Insights From the Global  Teaching InSights Video Study: A Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Maximilian Stark; Katrin Lohrmann; Marina Elena Pfeifer; Anne C. Frenzel
articles_hidden.abstract: Existing research into the link between teachers’ emotions and the quality of their lessons has generally relied either on students’ or teachers’ ratings of instructional quality and drawn on teacher samples from homogenous cultural contexts. The present study addressed these limitations by employing data from the multinational Global Teaching InSights study, in which 652 mathematics teachers in eight countries in East Asia, Europe, and South America self-reported their experiences of enjoyment, anger, and anxiety about teaching, and expert raters assessed instructional quality along the three established dimensions of classroom management, socialemotional support, and instructional support. We used fixed-effects linear models to obtain estimates for the covariation between self-reported trait emotions and observer-rated instructional quality dimensions. For social-emotional support, links with teacher anger and teacher anxiety were negative and significant; the link with teacher enjoyment was positive but did not reach statistical significance. These effects were largely homogenous across the international samples, as exploratory analyses revealed. For classroom management and instructional support, effects were negligible in size, and specifically teacher enjoyment–instructional support links were highly internationally heterogeneous. These findings provide essential insights into how teachers’ internal emotional experience translate into their outward instructional behaviors, and the nuances brought about by varying assessment approaches for instructional quality. The observed cross-country variability may spark future cross-national, cross-cultural research in this domain.

articles_hidden.title: Application of Bayesian Sequential Analyses to Single Case Data: A Proof-of-Principle Study
articles_hidden.authors: Simon Edward Blackwell; Pia Barisch; Michael Stumpp; Josefine Hirdes; Tobias Teismann; Jürgen Margraf; Marcella Lydia Woud
articles_hidden.abstract: Timely identification of whether a treatment is having the expected effect on symptoms could help improve outcomes and inform treatment personalization. Application of Bayesian sequential analysis to single case data may offer a useful method for rapidly identifying treatment success or failure at an individual level, tailored to an individual patient. This paper provides proof-of-principle for this concept, applied to simple internet-delivered interventions in an ABC randomized single case design. Seven participants with elevated symptoms of depression seeking treatment at an outpatient psychotherapy centre completed a two-week baseline period. They then completed two weeks of first one and then another internet-delivered cognitive training intervention, with the order of intervention randomized between participants. Participants rated depression symptoms on a daily basis throughout the study. Each participant’s baseline data was used to simulate hypothetical continuations after treatment initiation, and this in turn was used to determine individualised Bayes factor thresholds and other decision parameters for determining treatment success or failure. The study illustrates the potential application of sequential Bayesian analyses at a single case level to inform clinical decision-making, as well as highlighting potential challenges in implementing this approach.

articles_hidden.title: Has the prevalence of mental health problems of children and adolescents increased in recent 50 years? Systematic review and meta-analysis of repeated cross-sectional studies
articles_hidden.authors: Dirk Richter; Philipp Kerksieck; Christian Lauvrud; Anja I. Lehmann; Richard Whittington; Tom Whittington; Abbie Dickinson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: The treatment prevalence of mental health problems among children and adolescents has risen significantly in recent decades. It is unclear whether the increase in treatment prevalence is caused by changes in epidemiological prevalence.
Method: A systematic review and meta-analysis of repeated cross-sectional studies involving children and adolescents up to the age of 18 was conducted. The review included studies from around the world that were carried out using identical study designs at least twice in the same region.
Results: 58 publications were included, with data collected between 1973 and 2023. The overall odds ratio for changes in prevalence was 1.38 (95% confidence interval 1.26–1.52). This corresponds to a risk ratio of 1.32. The odds ratio for females was 1.47 (95% CI: 1.28–1.70), and the odds ratio for males was 1.25 (95% CI: 1.09–1.43). The greatest increase in prevalence was observed in the pandemic decade of 2020.
Discussion: The overall result corresponds to a 3.7% increase in prevalence over the entire 50-year period. This can be interpreted as a minor increase.
Conclusion: The rise in psychiatric treatment for children and adolescents is not primarily due to an increase in epidemiological prevalence.

articles_hidden.title: The ambiguous conceptualization of stress: stressor, stress response, and health outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Evelien Snippe; Solomiia Myroniuk; Malin Katja Meyer; Ute Bültmann; Susanne Scheibe; Bertus F. Jeronimus
articles_hidden.abstract: Stress is an umbrella term that lacks a universally agreed upon definition. The construct ambiguity of stress undermines theoretical integration, construct validity, and cumulative knowledge development. In our critical review, we trace the historical evolution of the stress construct, delineate sources of conceptual ambiguity, and evaluate whether the term stress itself is necessary for scientific exploration. We show that we do not need the term stress to describe the phenomena studied in stress research. However, the term ‘stress’ may still be useful to refer to a field of research and to integrate research findings. We demonstrate that phenomena related to stress can be described using more precise constructs: stressors, stress responses, and health outcomes. To facilitate conceptual clarity, we synthesize umbrella definitions for these constructs. Because such umbrella definitions remain necessarily broad, we emphasize that specifying the conceptualization and operationalization of the stressor, stress response, and health outcomes is indispensable for empirical rigor. To this end, we introduce the Stress Conceptualization Checklist for Empirical Studies (SuCCES), a structured reporting framework that guides researchers to describe the theory and conceptualization, specify which type of stressor, stress response and health outcome is studied, describe how they have arrived at their operationalization and differentiation  between the stressor, stress response and health outcomes, and specify the context, time scale, life period, and assessment window of their stress measurement. This reporting standard aims to strengthen construct validity, improve measurement coherence, and promote cumulative progress in research on stress-related processes.

articles_hidden.title: Peer effects on risk of psychiatric disorders: A nationwide study of Norwegian adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Ludvig Daae Bjørndal; Mathias Valstad; Espen Moen Eilertsen; Ziada Ayorech; Sverre Berg Ofstad; NA; Kenneth S. Kendler; Eivind Ystrom
articles_hidden.abstract:
Importance: Peers are hypothesized to influence adolescent mental health. However, most peer effects studies are susceptible to selection bias and reverse causation, limiting causal inference.
Objective: Examine classroom peer effects using a genetically informed approach and quasi-random classroom assignment.
Design, Setting, and Participants: Nationwide primary and specialist care registry data were used to follow a cohort of 750 750 Norwegian adolescents born between 1998 and 2010 until first registered psychiatric diagnosis, emigration, death, or December 31 2023. School class, school, and residential area at age 13 were identified. Data were analyzed from March to October 2026.
Exposures: (1) Pearson-Aitken Family-Genetic Risk Scores (FGRSs) indexing genetic liability to psychiatric disorders for individuals and peers sharing classroom, school, and/or residential area. Classrooms did not differ systematically in FGRSs, demonstrating that classroom peer FGRSs served as a natural experiment of quasi-randomization into peer environments. (2) Peers’ psychiatric diagnoses.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Registrations for alcohol use disorder (AUD), drug use disorder (DUD), major depression (MD), and anxiety diagnoses. Associations with classroom peer FGRSs and interaction effects with individual genetic liability and sex were estimated using discrete-time survival and Cox proportional hazards models.
Results: Psychiatric disorder risk was partly clustered at the classroom level (proportions of explained variance 0.9-5.0%). One SD increase in classroom risk was associated with a hazard ratio [HR] of 1.26 for AUD, 1.53 for DUD, and 1.18 for MD, and 1.20 for anxiety disorders. Classroom peer FGRSs were associated with increased risk of AUD in early adolescence (highest vs. lowest peer FGRS quintile, HR: 1.18; 95% CI 1.04, 1.34), MD (HR: 1.10; 95% CI, 1.06-1.14), and anxiety (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03-1.11). Classmate diagnoses were associated with elevated risk of DUD, MD, and anxiety (HRs: 1.02-1.16). No interaction effects between classroom peer FGRSs and genetic liability were observed; classroom peer FGRSs estimated for females predicted a higher risk among females (interaction HRs: 1.02-1.04). 
Conclusions and relevance: We found evidence of classroom peer effects, unbiased by selection bias and reverse causation, on internalizing disorder and AUD risk in early adolescence. Future studies are necessary to understand traits and mechanisms involved.

articles_hidden.title: The impact of level of automation and lighting conditions on drivers’ visual scanning patterns in an urban environment
articles_hidden.authors: Yee Thung Lee; Rafael C. Gonçalves; Ibrahim Ozturk; Albert Solernou; Karl Proctor; Natasha Merat
articles_hidden.abstract: Elevated crash risk is observed in manual driving after dark, partly because reduced visibility constrains drivers’ visual scanning patterns. L2 assisted driving technologies may help compensate for these increased attentional demands by reducing drivers’ physical operational demands, thereby freeing attentional resources that may support more extensive visual scanning. However, research on L2 has largely focused on daytime motorway scenarios, leaving it unclear how L2 may affect performance during after dark urban driving, where peripheral traffic places unique attentional demands on drivers under reduced visibility. This driving simulator study employed a 2 x 2 within-participants design to examine the effects of automation levels (manual driving, L2 assisted driving) and lighting conditions (daytime, after dark) on visual scanning patterns in urban scenarios. We also investigated whether visual attention towards different types of ambient traffic (vulnerable road users, parked vehicles) differed across conditions. Results showed that horizontal gaze dispersion did not differ across automation levels. However, percentage of glance time analysis showed that drivers spent more time monitoring the peripheral environments during L2 assisted driving than manual driving. Regardless of levels of automation, drivers allocated greater visual attention towards VRUs over parked vehicles, suggesting a consistent prioritisation of safety-relevant dynamic elements regardless of the attentional resources available to them. However, this pattern was only observed during daytime conditions, reflecting drivers’ reduced ability to distinguish between different elements of the driving scene under reduced visibility. L2 assisted driving also reduced vertical gaze dispersion relative to manual driving, though the reduction was less pronounced after dark, potentially because ambient traffic was only perceivable at closer distances under reduced visibility and therefore appeared lower in the visual field, requiring greater vertical scanning. These results imply that future driving assistance systems may benefit from incorporating night-vision camera systems to better support drivers’ visual attention in the dark.

articles_hidden.title: Are food odours special? A systematic review of food odours as experimental stimuli to study reward responses in human subjects
articles_hidden.authors: Leonie Seidel; Putu Agus Khorisantono; Germaine Pinckaers; Liv Hog; Janina Seubert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Food odours are often used to study anticipatory food reward, yet it remains unclear whether they evoke stronger reward responses than other odours or food cues presented in other sensory modalities. We systematically reviewed the literature to evaluate these assumptions.

Methods: MEDLINE, Embase and Web of Science were searched. Experimental studies investigating behavioural reward responses to orthonasal food odours in healthy participants were included. Two primary contrasts were considered: (1) food vs. non-food odours and (2) food odours vs. food stimuli, as well as the influence of hunger and satiety. Risk of bias was assessed using QualSyst and certainty of evidence using GRADE. A co-occurrence network of odours used in the field was constructed. 

Results: Of the 64 included studies, 11 compared food with non-food odours (total N = 363) statistically, while three compared food odours with pictures (total N = 216). Evidence for greater reward responses to food than non-food odours was limited and inconsistent, although positive findings tended to originate from larger studies. Evidence suggesting that food pictures elicit stronger reward responses than food odours was limited due to the small evidence base and methodological heterogeneity. Across studies, odour selection was concentrated on a small number of stimuli.

Conclusions: Few studies have directly examined assumptions underlying the use of food odours as reward stimuli. Greater methodological standardisation and explicit stimulus comparisons are needed to establish under which experimental conditions food odours provide an optimal model of anticipatory food reward. This work was funded by the ERC (grant agreement No. 947886) and registered at OSF.IO/237FW.
Keywords: odour, vision, food reward, hunger, satiety, network

articles_hidden.title: Persistent Belief Updating Despite Perfect Predictability – The Atypical Iterative Prior Updating Account Of Autism
articles_hidden.authors: Yun Wai Foo; Sonja Coenen; Christine Falter-Wagner; Zhuanghua Shi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Within predictive coding accounts of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), two competing explanations locate perceptual atypicalities within inference: weak prior formation versus altered weighting of prediction errors. We propose the atypical iterative prior updating (AIPU) account, which shifts the locus from inference to what happens afterwards: sensory evidence is overweighted during iterative belief updating over time. The accounts predict distinct temporal signatures of attentional divergence. 
Methods: To distinguish among the accounts, we presented autistic and typically developing adults with a distractor suppression paradigm using a 100%-valid spatial cue and varying distractor prevalence, while eye movements tracked the temporal dynamics of attentional selection. 
Results: Both groups showed equivalent first-fixation capture, ruling out prior-formation differences. Distractor prevalence modulated interference differently across groups. Autistic participants produced larger reaction time interference, more fixations, and more target refixations, a pattern emerging after initial selection. These findings locate ASD-related differences specifically in iterative updating across time, not in perceptual inference. 
Conclusions: The mechanism points to sustained attentional engagement: rather than terminating sensory sampling once expectations are confirmed, autistic individuals continue accumulating evidence even under perfect predictability. The world might feel "too much" not because perceptual inference is altered, but because updating continues beyond resolution.

articles_hidden.title: Outcomes of Preregistered Studies Related to Extra-Sensory Perception, and Mind-Matter Interaction: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Patrizio Tressoldi; Lance Storm
articles_hidden.abstract:
This review systematically examined preregistered studies on extrasensory perception (ESP) and mind-matter interaction (micropsychokinesis; i.e., micro-PK) available through October 2026. The primary aims were to evaluate their outcomes and compare the percentage of positive findings with those observed in mainstream psychology. We followed the PRISMA Guidelines. We searched major preregistration repositories, including the Open Science Framework and the Koestler Parapsychology Unit (KPU) Study Registry, and relevant meta-analyses. Inclusion criteria focused on completed studies with available preregistration and final results only for confirmatory hypotheses. A positive outcome was defined as the support of at least one confirmatory hypothesis, strictly following preregistered procedures and statistics without deviation. A total of 50 studies with a total of 60 experiments, met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Of these, 17 experiments (28.3%) reported a positive outcome, and 20 confirmatory hypotheses out of 97 (20.6%) were positive.
Interestingly, and contrary to some expectations, a broader comparison indicated that preregistered studies concerning ESP and PK did not necessarily exhibit a much lower proportion of confirmed hypotheses when compared with results for preregistered studies in mainstream psychology.

articles_hidden.title: What Helps or Hinders Therapeutic Relationships in Inpatient Mental Healthcare: a Systematic Review to Inform Policy and Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Ruth Cooper; Siying Li; Una Foye; Lara Levetan; Alessandro Dorata; Jude Beng; Winnie Liu; T K; Dawn Cutler; Jasmine Lee
articles_hidden.abstract:
