Background: Therapeutic relationships between service users and staff on inpatient mental health wards are central to the delivery of high-quality care and have been prioritised by policy makers. Yet these relationships are frequently found to be poor across inpatient settings, and more evidence is needed on how to foster good therapeutic relationships. In collaboration with lived experience researchers, we conducted a large systematic review, which was requested and carried out in partnership with NHS England, to identify facilitators and barriers to effective therapeutic relationships on inpatient wards. 

Methods: We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, HMIC (between January 1999-September 2025) for quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods primary research studies. Study quality was assessed using the Mixed Method Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Data were synthesised using an iterative analytic process, informed by framework analysis and narrative synthesis, across five interconnected levels: 1) individual (service user and staff experiences), 2) microsystem (daily interactions), 3) mesosystem (ward environment), 4) macrosystem (the wider organisation), 5) chronosystem (time and change across levels). 

Results: 184 studies with 19,984 participants (n=16,138 service users, n=3,846 staff) were included. Across study designs, four main categories emerged: 1) reducing power imbalances helped facilitate positive relationships and, conversely, restrictive practices damaged them; 2) staff relational skills including empathy, non-judgemental approaches and treating service users as individuals, rather than simply ‘patients’, helped build positive relationships; 3) staff continuity and time for staff to connect with service users was  critical to building positive relationships; ward contexts that prioritised task completion and/or were risk-focused weakened relationships; 4) ward environments that created opportunities to build interpersonal connections between staff and service users (e.g. shared spaces) strengthened relationships whereas those that provided limited opportunities for interaction weakened relationships. 

Conclusion: We identified four key factors that can help or hinder therapeutic relationships on mental health inpatient wards: power dynamics between staff and service users; restrictive practices; relational skills of staff; staff availability and consistency, and ward environments that facilitated interpersonal connections. We found evidence gaps particularly for minoritised ethnic communities and organisational influences. We suggest strategies which could help relationship building, including support with repairing relational ruptures, greater emphasis on relationship building in staff roles, and ward environments that support connection. 

Registration: The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (registration number: CRD420251047929).

articles_hidden.title: Consensus-based TRansparent, sUStainable, and Transferable (TRUST) best-practice guidelines for visual word recognition research
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Gagl; Xenia Schmalz; Karo Brimmers; Sascha Schroeder; Jascha Rüsseler; Fritz Günther; Monika Tschense; Silvia Brem; Marc Brysbaert; Hanna Woloszyn
articles_hidden.abstract: Reading is a fundamental life skill, and at its basis is the ability to process single words. Researchers often study single-word processing using lexical decision tasks. However, most research is conducted in a single language by separate research groups, limiting comparability, replicability, and generalizability. In addition, best-practice knowledge is often only transmitted informally within labs, leading to heterogeneity and reduced reproducibility across labs. Here, we, the TRUST Consortium, established a consensus-based research guideline for current best practices in psycholinguistic reading research by integrating expert knowledge. We used German as a case study and formulated guidelines for visual lexical decision experiments. We reached consortium-level consensus through multiple feedback circles and quantified agreement using importance ratings. The guidelines are openly available as a living guideline document on a webpage (\href{https://trust-guidelines-v01.readthedocs.io/en/latest/}{\textbf{trust-guidelines-v01.readthedocs.io}}), with git-versioning infrastructure that makes changes transparent and enables discussion. To validate the guidelines, we implemented the German Lexicon Project, providing an empirical feedback loop to test our suggestions. The living, open nature of the guidelines invites broader community feedback. It also enables future extension to other languages, groups (e.g., dyslexics), and methods (e.g., brain imaging), as it is openly available and includes instructions for hosting an adapted version at no cost. Thus, we provide a document intended to raise research standards in reading research worldwide, as a service to the community, potentially increasing replication rates and generalizability of relevant effects and phenomena.

articles_hidden.title: Do I experience anxiety, anger, and happiness in the same way as you do? A relational approach to emotion qualia across levels of alexithymia
articles_hidden.authors: Lin Lipeng; Zhang Chuyin; Naotsugu Tsuchiya
articles_hidden.abstract: Do people experience emotions in the same way? How can we characterize the sameness of emotional quality? Qualitative aspects of emotional experience are usually communicated through words. However, words can be ambiguous and can mean different things to different people. Here, we introduce a relational approach, which minimizes the reliance on language yet characterizes emotional experiences as structure, based on similarity judgments among emotion-evoking videos. This Registered Report will apply this method to characterize a psychological condition of “alexithymia,” which is described as “no words for emotions”. In two experiments, participants will rate the similarity between successive videos, based on the feelings evoked by the videos. Repeated video pairs will measure the degree of consistency in their similarity judgments. We will test whether individuals scoring high and low in alexithymia differ in the structure and consistency of their judgments. To disentangle the structures driven by sensory, rather than emotional, aspects of the videos, we will run a control experiment where participants rate the similarity of videos, ignoring the evoked emotions. A pilot study (N = 679) supports the feasibility of this design. By bypassing verbal reports, our approach can inform the study of emotional experience and help to clarify the nature of alexithymia.

articles_hidden.title: From Symptoms to Structures: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Major Depressive Symptom Networks
articles_hidden.authors: Charles Jack Strathdee; Phuong Linh Dang; isabel Krug; Litza Kiropoulos; Charles Benjamin Malpas
articles_hidden.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading condition examined using network analysis. However, meta-analytic evidence is limited for MDD symptom network studies. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses reporting guidelines, we searched Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL and bibliographies of previous literature for articles that have produced MDD symptom networks. After screening, 104 articles (N = 875,852) were included in this review, consisting of 85 cross-sectional and 19 temporal network analysis studies. A random-effects Meta-analytic Gaussian Network Aggregation (MAGNA) of MDD symptom networks was estimated based on available data. Despite a pronounced variation in MDD measures and sample demographics, findings consistently showed that depressed mood and fatigue emerged as the most central symptoms. Collectively, this systematic review and meta-analysis underscores network analysis as a technique for understanding MDD symptom dynamics and one that has the potential to improve psychological interventions. Ongoing efforts toward intensive longitudinal datasets and improved reporting practices represent two key avenues for MDD network analysis research.

articles_hidden.title: Neurofeedback of meditation states to close the loop between subjective experience and brain activity: Evaluating four neural markers
articles_hidden.authors: Henrik Röhr; Nursena Armagan; Luca Saini; Andreas Tzschaschel; Gabriel Salwey; Lukas Hecker; Daniel Andrew Atad; Marieke K. van Vugt; Stefan Schmidt; Fynn-Mathis Trautwein
articles_hidden.abstract: Neurofeedback creates a closed loop between subjective experience and brain activity. Such a feedback loop might allow establishing direct neuro-experiential correspondences, thereby narrowing the gap between the seemingly irreconcilable domains of private conscioussness and external measurement. We introduce a repeated-probing paradigm that allows systematic testing of such neuro-experiential correspondences within individuals by randomizing and blinding the feedback signal direction across trials, combined with semi-structured phenomenological interviews following unblinded regulation sessions. We apply this paradigm to electroencephalography (EEG) neurofeedback in experienced meditators across two studies. Study 1 (n=9) aimed to replicate the previously reported correspondence between posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) gamma activity and effortless awareness, extending the paradigm from visual to auditory feedback. An exploratory Study 2 (n=4) evaluated three additional markers: occipital alpha, midfrontal theta, and PCC high-beta power. In Study 1, participants identified the expected correspondence significantly above chance for both visual and auditory feedback (mean accuracy=72.5%). Additionally, gamma power was significantly reduced during neurofeedback-assisted meditation. In Study 2, no marker yielded significant neuro-experiential correspondences, although alpha power increased and high-beta power decreased during neurofeedback-assisted meditation. Phenomenological interviews revealed distinct meditative strategies, with releasing effort and control predominating in gamma neurofeedback. However, whole-brain and control analyses raised concerns about the spatial specificity and potential muscular contamination of the gamma signal. Our findings introduce a novel neurophenomenological neurofeedback paradigm, replicate and extend previous findings on the correspondence between effortless awareness and gamma feedback, and highlight important limitations in interpreting these effects as reflecting neural rather than muscular activity.

articles_hidden.title: Proactive Academic Stress Screening in Education: NPRO-8 Core Mental Fitness Screening
articles_hidden.authors: Jerome I. Rotgans
articles_hidden.abstract: Academic stress is a longstanding concern in education, with evidence linking it to examination difficulties, disrupted sleep, and poorer wellbeing. A student support pathway that depends on students requesting help or showing visible deterioration risks intervening only after difficulties have affected daily functioning. This paper proposes NPRO-8 Core as a new approach to proactive, objective assessment of stress-related functioning in students. Its preventive rationale is to create opportunities for recognition and support before difficulties escalate. A two-tier pathway combines brief screening offered across an institution with targeted functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) assessment during structured cognitive tasks. The assessment considers Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact, with repeated measurements intended to support review over time. Questionnaires provide access to students’ experiences; physiological and behavioural measures add a complementary perspective that does not depend solely on recognizing and reporting distress. The proposed contribution is to integrate these sources into a proactive student support pathway. Drawing on the preventive logic of physical-health screening, the framework links measurement to timely review and appropriate action.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Behavioral Signs: Toward a Multidomain Risk Architecture for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Pedro Salinas Quintana
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) prevalence has increased markedly over recent decades, yet primary tools for early detection remain focused almost exclusively on observable behavioral signs in children aged 18 months and older. Instruments such as the M-CHAT-R/F, ADOS-2, and ADI-R, while clinically valuable, operate within a narrow temporal and conceptual window that systematically excludes a wide range of prenatal, perinatal, medical, environmental, and psychosocial signals now supported by robust empirical evidence.

Objective: This paper presents a theoretically grounded critique of current early detection frameworks for ASD and proposes a Multidomain Early Risk Architecture (MERA). MERA is a detection architecture rather than a causal model of aetiology: it organizes ten empirically supported domains of clinically accessible signals according to the developmental window in which each becomes observable, and specifies through a four-tier taxonomy what inference each class of signal can bear.

Approach: A structured narrative synthesis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2006 and 2025 was conducted across PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science. Each retained source was mapped to one of 75 candidate risk factors and classified by study design and journal indexing quartile. The resulting evidence base comprises 152 factor–source pairings drawn from 148 distinct sources, organized into ten thematic domains and four evidential tiers.

Findings: The retained literature documents ASD-relevant signals distributed across all ten domains and four developmental windows. Sixty-nine percent of pairings derive from quartile-1 journals and 38 from systematic reviews or meta-analyses. Half of the evidence base corresponds to factors established before any behavioural observation of the child is possible, and which no current screening instrument incorporates. Domains differ systematically in evidential status: some comprise antecedent exposures, others early prodromal markers, and others features of the diagnostic phenotype itself or associated conditions of contested directionality.

Conclusion: A multidomain architecture that stratifies signals by developmental window and by evidential status offers a conceptual foundation for tiered developmental surveillance. The framework has implications for instrument development, primary care protocols, and public health policy—particularly in settings such as Chile where diagnostic delays remain substantial. Its domain structure and clinical utility require prospective validation, which the framework is explicitly designed to enable.

articles_hidden.title: Public support for policing gangs: normative, instrumental, and affective predictors of police empowerment in Aotearoa New Zealand
articles_hidden.authors: William Taylor; Julia Yesberg; Apriel D Jolliffe Simpson
articles_hidden.abstract: In many jurisdictions, police are periodically granted new powers intended to reduce crime and enhance community safety, raising questions about the conditions under which the public supports expanded police authority. The Gangs Act 2024 granted the New Zealand Police new powers to restrict gang activity, including the authority to arrest individuals for displaying gang insignia in public and to disperse gang gatherings in public spaces. Drawing on survey data from a non-representative sample of 766 adult residents of Aotearoa New Zealand, we examine normative (procedural justice and legitimacy), instrumental (police effectiveness and fear of crime), and affective predictors of public support for these powers. Affective responses (feeling safer at the prospect of the new powers) were the strongest predictor of support, and accounted for much of the association between the other predictors and support. Procedural justice was associated with support directly and indirectly, mainly via affective responses. Right-wing political orientation and fear of crime were associated with higher support, and interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals predicted lower support. Police effectiveness was positively correlated with support but negatively associated with it once fairness was accounted for. This study extends the police empowerment literature to the context of powers targeted at a specific, socially stigmatised group. Our findings suggest that support for such powers is more closely tied to how they make people feel than to judgements about police effectiveness, and that those with personal contact with gang-affiliated individuals are less supportive, raising questions about public opinion as a basis for justifying targeted police powers.

articles_hidden.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Vengeful: Evaluations of Standing up for Oneself versus Having Another’s Back
articles_hidden.authors: Catherine Stevenson; Marc Berman
articles_hidden.abstract: Bystander evaluations are a relatively unexplored area of retaliation, yet they are crucial to the reputations through which people navigate the social world. Further, though generally deriding harm, people are often forced to contend with it. By examining how people evaluate retaliation—or the choice not to retaliate—on behalf of self, friend, or stranger in various circumstances, we observed several interconnected results. We found that retaliation was favored when open and visible to offender and onlookers and also commensurate with the original offense and condemned when considered surreptitious and harsh. In addition, the more retaliation was endorsed, the more highly people rated retaliation for allies (friends) over self- and third-party retaliation. Conversely, in scenarios where retaliation was regarded more negatively, people judged abstaining from retaliation for oneself and others with greater approval. Notably, harsh retaliation—while judged negatively—produced both a deterrence effect and even suggested potential for future helping behavior. In conjunction with these findings, we predicted and found that loyalty is an important component in the mechanism underlying the evaluation of retaliation. Overall, the current studies suggest that retaliation may be the particular domain of allies—differing qualitatively from third-party retaliation—and is not a form of straightforward assistance.

articles_hidden.title: Using Behavioral Nudges to Engage Caregivers in Digital Shared Reading and Parenting Practices: Impacts on Caregivers and Early Childhood Development
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: This study is a mixed-methods impact evaluation of a digital parenting and shared book reading intervention (Worldreader’s BookSmart app with embedded parenting tips, Vroom TipsTM) on caregivers’ self-efficacy, beliefs, and practices, and early childhood outcomes in South Africa. We further investigated whether behavioral nudges could promote sustained engagement. Study 1 consisted of a 4-arm randomized controlled trial (BookSmart, BookSmart with reminder nudges, BookSmart with goal-setting nudges, control group) where caregivers (N = 519) of children aged 3-5 years used BookSmart for 15 weeks. We found randomization to access the intervention (i.e., intent-to-treat) had no significant effect on caregiver or child outcomes. However, behavioral nudges, particularly goal-setting messages, increased caregiver engagement and improved cognitive and language skills specifically for disadvantaged children (i.e., children from lower-SES households and children with lower baseline skills). Greater intervention engagement (i.e., treatment-on-the-treated) was significantly associated with language skills and marginally associated with literacy skills. Study 2 consisted of qualitative interviews with caregivers (N = 20) before and after using BookSmart for 3 weeks. Results indicated that several barriers impacted caregivers’ engagement with the intervention, including costs (e.g., airtime) and language accessibility (e.g., caregivers reported translating English books into their native language). Our results highlight that digital reading interventions have the potential to support early childhood development, while stressing that engagement with the intervention is critical in realizing potential positive outcomes. The findings suggest that access and usage barriers should be considered when designing interventions and that behavioral nudges may serve to increase engagement.
